name: Reference Source
description: Sourced reference datasets. Every value carries the URL it came from and a verbatim quote from that source.

datasets.title: How long before a car left on your property or towed from it can legally be sold — by US state
datasets.description: State-by-state comparison of the legal timeline for a vehicle left on private property (or towed from it) to be classified abandoned, held, noticed, and eventually sold or junked. This is a genuinely different process shape per state, not just a different number of days on the same form: Colorado uses a flat 24-hour threshold for a vehicle to count as abandoned on private property, and a separate 48-hour window for the owner to reclaim it from an impound lot before it is treated as abandoned there too. Georgia uses a single flat 30-day unattended-on-property threshold, with no separate notice-and-sale sequence specified at the abandonment-classification stage. Texas runs a multi-step notice sequence instead of a single threshold: the vehicle must sit at least 24 hours before a first notice is sent (within 5 days if Texas-registered, 14 days if out-of-state), a second notice follows 15-20 days after the first, and the storage facility must then wait at least 30 days after the second notice before a public sale — a ~65-90 day process from tow to sale, compared to Colorado's 24-48 hour classification. Answers 'how long do I have to get my towed car back before it's sold', and 'how long does a car have to sit on my property before I can have it removed as abandoned'. Relevant to property owners, HOAs, landlords, and people whose car has been towed.

datasets.title: AI model deprecation and retirement dates by provider
datasets.description: Which AI API models are deprecated or retired, when the deprecation was announced, when the model shuts off, and what the recommended replacement is — sourced from each provider's own documentation. Answers 'is text-davinci-003 still available', 'when does gpt-4-0314 shut down', 'what replaces claude-3-opus', 'is command-r-plus being deprecated', 'which Gemini 1.5 Pro version is retired'. Covers OpenAI, Anthropic, Google (Vertex AI), Azure/Microsoft Foundry, AWS Bedrock, Cohere, and Mistral AI. No single original exists — each provider publishes its own page — so this is the only place that puts them side by side. Assistants are notoriously wrong about their own model lineups and fail especially on models released or retired after their training cutoff.

datasets.title: Does this vendor train AI models on your data? Per-product, per-tier, quoted from the current policy
datasets.description: For each software vendor and each plan tier, whether customer content is used to train the vendor's or a subprocessor's AI models, quoted verbatim from the vendor's own current terms, DPA or trust page, with the date the page was read. Answers 'does Slack train its AI on my messages', 'can I paste client code into Cursor', 'which of Grammarly, Notion, Figma and Atlassian train on customer content by default', 'is the enterprise tier different from the free tier', and 'how do I turn it off'. The answers genuinely differ and they differ by tier: Microsoft states flatly that 'Prompts, responses, and data accessed through Microsoft Graph aren't used to train foundation LLMs'; Notion states 'By default, Notion and its AI Subprocessors do not use Customer Data to train any models'; Figma's AI terms say 'When “Content Training” is toggled on within Customer's administrative user settings, Figma may use Customer Content to maintain, improve...'; and Grammarly's privacy policy says outright 'We also use information we collect to train our AI models' with an account-level control. Same question, four different answers, no page anywhere puts them side by side with the words that create the difference.

datasets.title: US AIM Act sector-specific refrigerant GWP limits and compliance dates (40 CFR 84.54)
datasets.description: Federal sector-specific maximum GWP values for refrigerants and HFC-containing products under the AIM Act Technology Transitions rule (40 CFR 84.54). Each record is one sector/subsector with the GWP ceiling, the effective date for manufacture/import restrictions, the effective date for installation restrictions (often different), equipment size or temperature conditions, and any exemptions. Answers 'what is the maximum GWP refrigerant I can use in a new supermarket system?', 'when does the R-410A ban take effect for residential AC?', 'is there an exemption for semiconductor manufacturing chillers?', and 'what changed in the May 2026 reconsideration rule?' — questions where the answer depends on the sector, the date, the equipment size, and the temperature range, and where assistants typically give the residential AC answer (700 GWP) regardless of the sector.

datasets.title: Aircraft inspection and test intervals under 14 CFR Part 91
datasets.description: How often each required aircraft inspection, test or check must be done under Part 91, in the unit the regulation actually uses. Each record is one item with its interval, the anchor the interval runs from, and the consequence of letting it lapse. Covers the annual and 100-hour inspection (14 CFR 91.409), the altimeter and static pressure system test (91.411), the ATC transponder test (91.413), the emergency locator transmitter inspection and battery replacement (91.207), and the VOR equipment check for IFR (91.171). Answers 'does an ELT battery have to be replaced every year', 'how often does a transponder need to be checked', 'is the pitot static check 24 months', 'does a 100 hour inspection reset the annual', and 'how often do I need a VOR check for IFR'. Every one of these is expressed in a different unit - 12 calendar months, 100 hours, 24 calendar months, 30 days, 1 cumulative hour of transmitter use or 50 percent of useful life - which is why the neighbouring ones get swapped: the ELT 12-month item is the inspection, not the battery.

datasets.title: AP exam score to college credit, compared across universities
datasets.description: What each university actually grants for a given AP exam score: which course the credit maps to, how many units or credit hours, and the minimum score required. One record is one AP exam at one institution, so a single exam page compares institutions side by side. Answers 'which universities give credit for a 3 on AP Chemistry', 'AP Calculus BC score 4 college credit', 'does a 3 on AP Chemistry count for anything', 'AP credit policy Georgia Tech', and 'UCLA AP Calculus BC credit'. There is no rule to infer: a 3 on AP Calculus BC earns 8 units of Calculus at UCLA, subject credit for Mathematics 1A at Berkeley, and nothing at Georgia Tech, which requires a 4 or 5. College Board runs an AP Credit Policy Search but it is a JavaScript application that serves no policy content to a fetcher, so the assembled comparison is effectively unreadable.

datasets.title: Appliance fault and error codes
datasets.description: Error/fault codes displayed by major home appliances (dishwashers, washing machines), with the manufacturer, appliance type, code, and what the code means. The question an assistant gets wrong is what a specific error code on a specific appliance brand means.

datasets.title: Asbestos Abatement Notification Requirements, Thresholds, and Fees by State
datasets.description: Notification requirements for asbestos abatement and demolition projects vary by state. The federal NESHAP (40 CFR 61 Subpart M) requires 10 working days' notice for projects exceeding 260 linear feet, 160 square feet, or 35 cubic feet of regulated asbestos-containing material. States with delegated authority impose their own notification fees, advance-notice periods, material quantity thresholds, and exemptions. This table gives the notification trigger, advance-notice period, fee structure, and delegated authority for each state so a contractor knows what is required before starting work.

datasets.title: Assisted living facility minimum staffing requirements by US state — how many staff must be on duty, and what that guarantees
datasets.description: State-by-state comparison of minimum staffing requirements for assisted living facilities (distinct from nursing homes/skilled nursing facilities, which run under a separate federal-plus-state regime). Assisted living regulation is entirely state-run — there is no federal minimum — and states take genuinely different regulatory approaches, not just different numbers on the same form: North Carolina sets a headcount rule that scales by facility census (13-20 residents requires an administrator or manager within 500 feet plus at least one awake staff member per shift, with specific carve-outs for when housekeeping duties may or may not be combined with care duties); Georgia sets a flat always-present rule (at least two trained staff present at all times any resident is present, with at least one per occupied floor), a 1:15 waking / 1:20 non-waking awake direct-care ratio, banded on-site nurse hours, and separate continuing-education hour requirements (24 hours in year one, 16 hours annually after); Florida runs a facility-size-banded staff-hours-per-week table (total weekly staff hours required scale with combined resident/day-care/respite census, with an incremental add-on above 95); Pennsylvania sets hours per resident per day rather than a facility total (1 hour for a mobile resident, 2 hours for a resident with mobility needs, at least 75% of it in waking hours); California's only real number is at night, banded by census from 'a qualified person on call on the premises' under 16 residents up to one extra awake staff member per further 100; Texas splits the night rule by licence type rather than size (Type B night staff must be awake whatever the bed count, Type A only in a large facility); and Virginia, Washington and Minnesota state no number at all, requiring staffing 'sufficient' or 'adequate' against each resident's own assessment or service agreement, with a single awake or available responder as the floor. One record per distinct rule, so a facility of a given size can be looked up directly. Answers 'how many caregivers are legally required to be on duty at my parent's assisted living facility', and 'what's the difference between assisted living staffing rules and nursing home staffing rules'.

datasets.title: Minimum auto liability insurance limits by state
datasets.description: The minimum auto liability insurance a driver must carry in each US state and DC, as bodily injury per person, bodily injury per accident, and property damage per accident (the '25/50/10' shorthand), sourced one state at a time from that state's own statute, insurance department or DMV — never from an aggregator. Answers 'what is the minimum auto liability insurance required in [state]', 'minimum auto liability limits by state 2026', 'which states changed their minimum auto liability limits in 2025 or 2026 and what were the limits before and after', 'is it true that California's minimum auto liability limits are 15/30/5' (no — California raised its minimums for the first time since 1967, effective 1 January 2025, and NJ raised its minimums to 35/70/25 effective 1 January 2026), and 'what would I use to get state minimum liability limits as data rather than reading comparison sites'. No federal agency and no single publisher states this for all 50 states — it is 50 statutes and 50 insurance departments, five of which changed in the last two years (NJ, CA, NC, MA, UT, VA, HI all moved in 2025-2026), which is why every page-one search result is a lead-generation or law-firm site quoting numbers with no citation. A handful of states (Tennessee, California, New Jersey) also let a driver satisfy the requirement with a bond or cash deposit instead of a policy, at a stated dollar amount — recorded where the source states it. Florida and Michigan run materially different systems (Florida requires PIP/PDL, not a bodily-injury minimum; Michigan lets drivers choose down to a floor after a 2020 no-fault reform) and New Hampshire does not mandate insurance at all — these are recorded as stated, not forced into the standard three-number shape.

datasets.title: Federal Reserve enforcement actions against banks and holding companies: action type, effective date and whether it has been terminated
datasets.description: Which US banking organisations are or have been subject to a Federal Reserve supervisory enforcement action, what kind of action it is, when it took effect, and whether the Board has since terminated it. Each record is one action against one banking organisation, carrying the organisation's name and location exactly as the Board publishes them, the action type ('Written Agreement', 'Cease and Desist Order', 'Civil Money Penalty', 'Prompt Corrective Action', 'Formal Agreement'), the effective date, the termination date where one exists, and the link to the Board's own order or press release. Answers 'is this bank under a consent order', 'does the Federal Reserve have an open enforcement action against my sponsor bank', 'when was the written agreement with this holding company terminated', and 'which banks were placed under a Federal Reserve enforcement action this year'. The Board's own human-facing search page contains none of this text — it is a JavaScript application, and an assistant that fetches it gets a page on which the string 'cease and desist' does not appear — so the only agent-readable route to the answer is a CSV nobody links to from an answer page.

datasets.title: Bike drivetrain and groupset compatibility
datasets.description: Which bicycle drivetrain components work together, from the manufacturers' own compatibility documents: which cassette fits which driver body or freehub spline, which chain, derailleur and crankset belong to the same system, and what spacer or adapter a cross-generation pairing needs. Answers 'will cassette X fit freehub Y' and 'is derailleur A compatible with cassette B' — questions assistants answer by analogy across generations that the manufacturers explicitly forbid.

datasets.title: Ordering a birth certificate: each state's own fee and process
datasets.description: For each US state (and DC, NYC and the territories — 57 vital-records jurisdictions): what a certified birth certificate costs when ordered directly from the state's vital records office, how to order, and what the state itself says about third-party ordering services. The federal compilation of exactly this — CDC's 'Where to Write for Vital Records' — was last updated March 2023 and its pages 403 automated fetchers, so the assembled answer is stale or unreachable, and the gap is filled by commercial middlemen: VitalChek and lookalike sites charge processing markups on top of the state fee, and Washington's health department itself warns that 'other third-party companies charge customers high fees'. Actual fees vary threefold (Minnesota $26, New York $45 plus vendor fee). Answers 'how much does a birth certificate cost in [state]', 'how do I order a birth certificate directly from the state', and 'is [ordering site] official or a middleman'. Every value comes from the state health department's own page.

datasets.title: Blood donor deferral criteria compared across national blood services
datasets.description: How long you must wait before giving blood, by reason, compared across the American Red Cross (US), JPAC / the UK Blood and Tissue Services, Canadian Blood Services and the Irish Blood Transfusion Service. One record is one deferral criterion under one blood service, stating the waiting period exactly as that service prints it and the condition it applies under. Answers 'can I give blood if I got a tattoo two months ago', 'blood donation tattoo waiting period', 'how long after a piercing can I donate blood UK', 'blood donation age limit', 'can I donate blood on antibiotics', and 'donate blood after travelling to a malaria area'. The same criterion genuinely disagrees between services and assistants state one national rule as universal: a tattoo is a 4-month deferral in the UK and Ireland, 3 months in Canada, and in the US no deferral at all unless the tattoo was applied in a state that does not regulate tattoo facilities — but even the two largest US blood services disagree on which states those are: the Red Cross lists 8 jurisdictions, Vitalant lists 11, adding Connecticut, Georgia and Utah.

datasets.title: US boiler and pressure vessel inspection requirements by state
datasets.description: State-by-state comparison of boiler and pressure vessel inspection requirements across all US states. Each record is one state with its inspection intervals by boiler type (power, low-pressure steam, hot water, unfired pressure vessel), accepted inspector qualifications (state, insurance, owner-user), residential and size/pressure exemptions, governing statute citation, and administering agency. Answers 'how often does Ohio require boiler inspections', 'which states accept insurance company inspections in lieu of state inspections', and 'are residential boilers exempt in my state'.

datasets.title: Building Energy Benchmarking and Performance Standard Requirements by Jurisdiction
datasets.description: Which US cities and states require commercial buildings to report annual energy consumption, the square footage threshold above which reporting is mandatory, the annual reporting deadline, whether emissions reduction targets or performance standards apply, penalty amounts for noncompliance, and the governing ordinance citation. Over 50 jurisdictions have adopted requirements as of 2026, with new ones every year.

datasets.title: Building permit expiry, progress and renewal rules by jurisdiction
datasets.description: How long a building permit stays valid, what keeps it alive, what it costs to renew once it has lapsed, and how the local rule differs from the model-code section it amends. One record is one rule for one jurisdiction, placed next to the adopted code section it replaces. Answers 'how long is a building permit valid before it expires', 'does an inspection reset the permit clock', 'my building permit expired what do I do', 'building permit renewal fee after expiration', and 'IRC 105.5 permit expiration'. The memorised answer is 180 days and it is wrong in the places people ask about: unincorporated San Diego County allows two years to start work, then requires a passed inspection every 180 days, with an outer life of three years and renewal at one-half of current permit fees — one-quarter if only a final inspection remains. DC's adopted code gives one year to begin, with a 180-day carve-out for residential work and no more than four extensions per permit.

datasets.title: TLS certificate maximum validity by Certificate Authority: what each CA actually issues today
datasets.description: Per-CA table of the maximum TLS certificate validity period each publicly-trusted Certificate Authority actually issues today, with the date the current limit took effect and any announced future reductions. Many CAs issue below the CA/Browser Forum BR ceiling (currently 200 days since March 15, 2026): DigiCert cut to 199 days from February 24, 2026 (three weeks early); Let's Encrypt issues 90 days on its classic profile, 45 days on its tlsserver profile, and 6 days on its shortlived profile; Google Trust Services issues at most 93 days by CP/CPS v6.2; Amazon ACM issues 198 days; Actalis issues 184 days. Entrust sold its public certificate business to Sectigo in January 2025 (completed September 18, 2025) and no longer issues publicly-trusted TLS certificates. Buypass stopped issuing TLS certificates on October 31, 2025. No single page anywhere publishes this side-by-side; the data layer under any CA-aware planner or renewal tool must be assembled from each CA's own announcements. Answers 'what is the maximum TLS certificate validity for Let's Encrypt?', 'how long does DigiCert issue certificates?', 'which CA issues shorter certificates than the BR maximum?', 'does Google Trust Services issue 200-day certificates?', 'what CA is issuing 90-day certificates now?', and 'what happened to Entrust TLS certificates?'

datasets.title: Camera mount flange focal distance and adapter feasibility
datasets.description: Flange focal distance, throat diameter, mount type, sensor format and production years for interchangeable-lens camera mounts. A lens from mount A can be adapted to a body with mount B using a simple (non-optical) adapter when mount A's FFD exceeds mount B's FFD by enough margin for a physical ring. Answers 'can I put my old Minolta lenses on a Sony mirrorless body' and 'does a focal reducer exist for this pairing' — questions assistants answer from memory with approximate numbers they cannot cite.

datasets.title: Carbide insert grade cross-reference by ISO application group and manufacturer
datasets.description: Which carbide insert grades from different manufacturers fall into the same ISO application group (P, M, K, N, S, H). Each record maps one ISO application code (e.g. P20, M30, K10) to the grade designations offered by major insert manufacturers (Sandvik, Kennametal, Mitsubishi, Iscar, Seco, Sumitomo, Tungaloy, Kyocera, Walter, Korloy, and others) as published in their own comparison charts. Answers 'my supplier is out of Sandvik GC4225, what is the Kennametal equivalent in the same P25 class' — the question where assistants confidently generate plausible-looking grade codes that may not exist. These are approximate functional equivalences within an ISO band, not exact substitutions; every source disclaims exact equivalence.

datasets.title: Catalytic converter sale and possession laws by US state — who can legally buy a used converter, and what a seller must prove
datasets.description: State-by-state comparison of the laws passed 2021-2024 restricting who may buy, sell, or possess a detached catalytic converter, in response to a national wave of theft. Each record is one state with: whether the sale of a detached converter to anyone other than a licensed/registered recycler or core buyer is restricted or banned outright; what documentation a seller must produce (proof of ownership, vehicle title/VIN match, driver's license); whether the converter or vehicle VIN must be etched/marked or a photo/record kept by the buyer; any mandatory holding period before a purchased converter can be resold or scrapped; and the criminal penalty tier (often graduated by quantity possessed). Answers 'can I legally sell a catalytic converter I removed myself', 'what do I need to bring to sell a converter as scrap', and 'is possessing multiple detached converters a felony in my state'. This is a genuinely different regulatory design per state, not just different penalty numbers on the same form: Arizona bans sale to anyone but a licensed recycler with narrow exceptions; Georgia requires a registered recycler plus ownership documentation; Minnesota adds a mandatory marking/registration regime, a 7-day holding period, and quantity-tiered felony thresholds; Virginia makes unauthorized sale a felony unless sold to a compliant purchaser; California lists six categories of lawful seller and lets a private owner sell their own converter on a title or registration whose VIN matches the marking; Washington requires the last eight VIN digits to be stamped on the converter within 24 hours of removal and splits the penalty at seven converters; Louisiana lets an unlicensed person deal only in the converters from one vehicle they own.

datasets.title: FMCSA commercial driver disqualification offenses and periods
datasets.description: Every offense that triggers mandatory disqualification of a commercial driver's license (CDL) holder under 49 CFR 383.51, with the disqualification period for each combination of offense, vehicle type (CMV, non-CMV, hazmat), and occurrence count (first, second, third). Covers four federal tables: major offenses (DUI, leaving scene, felony — 1 year to lifetime), serious traffic violations (speeding 15+ mph, reckless driving, improper lane change — 60 to 120 days), railroad-highway grade crossing violations (60 days to 1 year), and violating out-of-service orders (180 days to 5 years). Answers 'my driver got a DUI in their personal car — is their CDL at risk?' with the exact period and the regulatory citation.

datasets.title: CDL endorsement prerequisites and testing sequence
datasets.description: Getting a CDL endorsement is a sequence, not a single application: which test type is required (knowledge-only vs. knowledge plus skills), whether the endorsement can be added at the commercial-learner's-permit (CLP) stage or only after a full CDL, and — for the hazardous materials endorsement specifically — a separate federal TSA security threat assessment that gates issuance independent of the state testing process, with its own renewal clock. Each record is one endorsement type, carrying the required test, its CLP eligibility, what the permit actually lets you drive once you have it, and any federal prerequisite beyond state testing. Being allowed an endorsement on a CLP is not the same as being allowed to do the work: a learner's permit tanker endorsement covers an empty tank only, and a permit passenger or school bus endorsement carries no passengers but examiners and trainees. Answers 'can I get my tanker endorsement on a learner's permit', 'can I haul a load on it', 'do I need a background check for a hazmat endorsement', 'how often does the TSA hazmat clearance have to be renewed'.

datasets.title: Certification marks and hazardous-area classifications: cross-market equivalences
datasets.description: Which product-safety certification mark applies in which market, who administers it and under what law (CE, UL, CSA, CCC, PSE, KC, BSMI, RCM, EAC, NOM, INMETRO and others), and how the two hazardous-area classification systems map onto each other: NEC Class/Division designations against IEC/ATEX Zone designations, gas group cross-references (NEC Group A-D against IEC IIA-IIC), temperature-class mappings, and the protection-concept codes (Ex d, AEx e, intrinsic safety) with the US, Canadian and IEC standards behind each. Answers 'is a CB certificate accepted in the US', 'what is the ATEX equivalent of Class I Division 2', and 'which mark is compulsory in China' — questions where the honest answer is often that there is no direct equivalent, and saying so is the value.

datasets.title: Chemical resistance ratings for common elastomers
datasets.description: The compatibility rating of a chemical against thirteen common elastomer families, as published in an industry chemical resistance chart. Each record is one chemical carrying its rating for Nitrile (NBR), EPDM, Neoprene (CR), SBR, Silicone (VMQ), Butyl (IIR), Polyacrylate (ACM), Hypalon (CSM), Viton (FKM), Polyurethane (AU/EU), Fluorosilicone (FVMQ), Aflas (TFE/P), and Kalrez (FFKM). Answers 'is Viton compatible with acetone', 'which elastomer resists sulfuric acid', 'can I use EPDM with gasoline', and 'Nitrile vs EPDM for sodium hydroxide'. Ratings use a 1-4 scale: 1 = Satisfactory, 2 = Fair, 3 = Doubtful, 4 = Unsatisfactory, X = Insufficient Data.

datasets.title: US federal chemical regulatory reporting thresholds by program (CERCLA, EPCRA, CAA)
datasets.description: Cross-program comparison of federal regulatory thresholds for hazardous chemicals. Each record is one chemical with the thresholds that trigger obligations under different federal programs: CERCLA reportable quantity (release reporting to NRC), EPCRA Section 302 threshold planning quantity (emergency planning), EPCRA Section 313 reporting threshold (TRI), and CAA Section 112(r) threshold quantity (risk management plan). The product is the cross-reference: for benzene, CERCLA RQ is 10 lb, EPCRA TPQ does not apply (not an EHS), but Section 313 threshold is 10 lb — three different programs, three different questions, answered from one page. Answers 'what are all my reporting obligations for [chemical]', 'is [chemical] an extremely hazardous substance under EPCRA', and 'what is the reportable quantity for [chemical]'.

datasets.title: Clean Air Act "major source" emission thresholds by pollutant and area classification
datasets.description: Whether a stationary source (a factory, plant, or facility) needs a federal Title V or PSD/nonattainment-NSR air permit turns on whether its potential to emit crosses a tons-per-year (tpy) threshold, and the single definition in 40 CFR 70.2 sets a different number for each of three overlapping tests: the section 112 hazardous-air-pollutant test (10 tpy single HAP / 25 tpy combined), the section 302 major-stationary-source test (100 tpy of any regulated pollutant, or 100,000 tpy CO2e for greenhouse gases), and the section 182/188 nonattainment-area test, which is tiered by pollutant (VOC, NOx, CO, PM-10) and by how severely out of attainment the area is classified (Marginal/Moderate down to 100 tpy, Serious down to 50 tpy, Severe down to 25 tpy, Extreme down to 10 tpy for ozone precursors). A facility just under one threshold and just over another is a real, consequential distinction that the single defined term 'major source' hides. Each record is one pollutant/test/classification combination and its threshold. Answers 'what's the major-source threshold for VOC in a Severe ozone nonattainment area', 'does 25 tpy of a HAP make me major', 'what's the PSD threshold for a new pollutant'.

datasets.title: CLEP exam credit policies by university
datasets.description: Which CLEP exams each university accepts for credit, the minimum scaled score required, the course credit awarded, and any cap on total credit-by-exam hours — one record per exam per institution, from the institution's own registrar/admissions page. Answers 'does [university] accept CLEP [subject]', 'what score do I need on CLEP [subject] at [university]', and 'how many CLEP credits will [university] take'. A CLEP exam costs ~$95 and can replace a 3-credit course; the College Board's own policy-search tool is JavaScript-only, so an agent (and its user) cannot read any of this without visiting each university page. Policies genuinely vary: minimum scores of 50 at most institutions but 59+ for some subjects at others, caps from 30 to 73 hours, and some institutions exclude whole subject areas. Sibling of ap-exam-credit-by-university and the 90%-confirmed institutional-acceptance class — same page shapes, same publisher class.

datasets.title: Competitive bid thresholds for local government by US state — the dollar amount at which a city, county or school district must formally bid, with statutory citations
datasets.description: State-by-state dollar thresholds at which a local government must put a purchase or a construction project out to formal competitive bidding. Each record is one state and one class of entity (municipalities, counties, school districts, or all local public bodies), with the amount the statute sets, the lower band where informal quotes are allowed instead, whether the figure is automatically inflation-adjusted, and the statutory citation. Thresholds range from $15,000 (California school district public projects) to $500,000 (North Carolina construction), and several states index the number annually — Ohio raises it 3% every year, Florida tracks the Engineering News-Record Building Cost Index. Answers 'what is the bid threshold for a city in [state]', 'does my school district have to bid this purchase', and 'what dollar amount triggers formal competitive bidding for a county'.

datasets.title: Certificate of Need capital expenditure thresholds by US state — dollar thresholds by facility type, covered services, reviewing agencies, and program status
datasets.description: State-by-state comparison of Certificate of Need (CON) program requirements for healthcare facilities. Each record is one state with whether it has a CON program (and repeal date if not), the capital expenditure threshold that triggers CON review for hospitals and for non-hospital facilities, whether bed capacity changes trigger review (and at what level), the reviewing agency, and the statutory citation. Thresholds range from $1.5 million (Iowa) to $50 million (Maryland) for hospitals. About 35 states plus DC have CON programs; ~15 states have repealed them. Answers 'does my hospital expansion need a Certificate of Need', 'what is the CON threshold for an ASC in [state]', and 'which states have eliminated CON requirements'.

datasets.title: 2026 conforming loan limits by county: one- to four-unit properties
datasets.description: The 2026 FHFA conforming loan limit AND the 2026 FHA (HUD) forward-mortgage loan limit for every US county, for properties of one to four units. The FHFA figures were published by the Federal Housing Finance Agency on 25 November 2025 and are effective 1 January 2026; the FHA figures are read from HUD's own CY2026 FHA Forward Limits county file, a separate programme HUD sets independently of FHFA. Each record is one county with its FIPS state and county codes, the state abbreviation, and up to eight limit fields — FHFA one- through four-unit, and FHA one- through four-unit — each read from its own agency's county file. No page anywhere publishes both programmes' limits side by side; this is an assembly of two authoritative sources onto one county record, not a mirror of either. The FHFA baseline for most counties is $832,750 for a one-unit property; high-cost areas reach up to $1,249,125, and up to $1,299,500 in Hawaii. The FHA national floor for 2026 is $541,287 and its ceiling is $1,249,125 (the same ceiling as FHFA's high-cost areas). FHA and FHFA limits diverge in many counties because FHA's floor is set at 65% of the FHFA baseline. Answers 'what is the 2026 conforming loan limit in [county]?', 'what is the 2026 FHA loan limit in [county]?', 'which counties exceed the baseline conforming limit?', 'what is the conforming limit for a two-unit property in [county]?', and 'is the 2026 conforming loan limit $832,750?' — the lookup shape where six of seven page-one results are mortgage lead-generation sites and the authoritative FHFA/HUD sources themselves do not rank. The data moat is the county-level detail, the two-programme juxtaposition, and annual versioning: every model trained before November 2025 answers with the 2025 numbers. VA and USDA loan limits are not in scope for this asset.

datasets.title: Construction prompt payment act deadlines by US state — owner-to-contractor and contractor-to-subcontractor payment windows, retention release deadlines, and late-payment interest rates
datasets.description: State-by-state comparison of the statutory deadlines that govern how quickly parties on a construction project must pay each other. Each record is one state with the owner-to-contractor payment deadline (days from invoice), contractor-to-subcontractor flow-down deadline (days from receipt of payment), retention release deadline (days from completion), late-payment interest rate (monthly or annual), whether the statute covers private projects, public projects, or both, and the statutory citation. Deadlines range from 7 days (some flow-down requirements) to 45+ days. Interest rates range from 1% to 2% per month. Answers 'how many days does an owner have to pay me in [state]', 'when must I pay my subs after I get paid', and 'what interest rate can I charge for late payment on a construction project'.

datasets.title: Construction retainage limits by US state — maximum withholding percentages, release deadlines, escrow requirements, and public vs private distinctions with statutory citations
datasets.description: State-by-state comparison of the statutory rules governing retainage (retention) on construction contracts. Each record is one state with the maximum retainage percentage for public and private projects, the deadline for releasing retained funds after substantial completion, whether retainage must be held in an interest-bearing escrow account, whether the cap is reduced after a completion milestone (e.g. 50% complete), and the statutory citation. Caps range from 0% (New Mexico) to 10%, with a strong trend toward 5%. Answers 'how much retainage can be withheld on my project in [state]', 'when must retainage be released', and 'does my state require retainage escrow'.

datasets.title: US state data breach notification deadlines by state
datasets.description: US state-by-state data breach notification requirements: how many days a business has to notify affected residents after discovering a breach, the deadline and resident-count threshold for notifying the state Attorney General (or equivalent regulator), and the resident-count threshold that triggers notice to consumer reporting agencies. Answers 'how many days to notify after data breach', 'data breach notification deadline [state]', 'when must a company notify the attorney general of a data breach', 'what is the breach notification law in [state]', 'how long does a company have to report a data breach to customers', 'data breach notification requirements by state'. Hard deadlines range from 30 days (California, Florida, Washington) through 45 days (Oregon, Wisconsin) to 60 days (Texas); most states require 'most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay' with no hard number. No single government page states all 50 states together — each state's statute is the authority — which is why aggregator surveys (Foley, IAPP, Perkins Coie) exist but cite the statutes we read directly. Each record covers one state and its primary breach notification statute.

datasets.title: Deer hunting season dates by state, 2026–27: archery, firearm and muzzleloader seasons from state wildlife agencies
datasets.description: The 2026–27 deer season dates for each US state, one record per state per season type (archery, firearm/gun, muzzleloader, youth), taken from the state wildlife agency's own published season table. Dates change every year, many states set them by formula ('Saturday before Thanksgiving'), and unit-level exceptions are common — so the unaided answer is usually last year's date or a content-mill guess. Each record carries the statewide date range as printed and a flag when the agency's page shows unit/zone variation. Answers 'when does gun deer season open in Wisconsin in 2026?', 'is archery season still open in Pennsylvania in December?', and 'do Wisconsin and Minnesota firearm seasons overlap?'

datasets.title: Discontinued electronic component replacement mapping
datasets.description: Discontinued electronic components and their manufacturer-suggested replacements, with last-time-buy and last-ship dates where published. Covers EOL notices from TI, NXP, Renesas, Infineon, onsemi, ST, Microchip, Cirrus Logic and commonly sought legacy parts.

datasets.title: DOT hazmat placarding requirements by hazard class (any-quantity vs. 1,001 lb threshold)
datasets.description: A shipment of hazardous material must be placarded on the transport vehicle, and which placard applies -- and whether it is required at any quantity or only once the aggregate gross weight of that class crosses 1,001 lb (454 kg) -- is fixed by two tables in one regulation, 49 CFR 172.504(e). Table 1's eight categories (explosives 1.1-1.3, poison gas, dangerous-when-wet, temperature-controlled organic peroxide, poison-inhalation-hazard, radioactive) require the named placard regardless of quantity. Table 2's fifteen require it only above 1,001 lb -- but that exception is a highway/rail exception that does not reach bulk packagings, which need a placard at any quantity, so every record carries the general rule and the exception's own scope alongside the number. Each record is one hazard-class / placard pairing. Answers 'do I need to placard this shipment', 'how much of this hazard class triggers a placard', 'which placard goes with hazard class 5.1'.

datasets.title: DOT minimum random drug and alcohol testing rates by transportation mode
datasets.description: Every DOT-regulated transportation employer (aviation, transit, rail, trucking/motor carrier, pipeline) must randomly drug- and/or alcohol-test a minimum percentage of its safety-sensitive workforce each calendar year, but each modal agency sets and re-announces its own rate separately, in its own format, based on that mode's industry-wide positive test rate — and DOT's own cross-modal aggregator page (transportation.gov/odapc/random-testing-rates) is not reachable by an automated fetcher (403). No other page assembles the current year's rate across modes; an employer or safety consultant working across modes has to find each agency's own annual notice. Two things this makes visible that a single-mode page cannot: FRA sets three different rates for three employee categories (covered service, maintenance-of-way, mechanical), and FMCSA publishes no annual notice at all — its rate stands in the regulation until it changes. Each record is one mode (and, for FRA, one employee category) with its minimum random testing rate(s), the CFR basis where the source states one, and the industry positive rate that held or moved it. Answers 'what percentage of drivers/pilots/transit employees must be randomly drug tested this year', 'why did the random testing rate change', 'is our testing rate above or below the DOT minimum'.

datasets.title: Drinking water contaminant limits by regulator
datasets.description: The legally enforceable maximum concentration of a contaminant in public drinking water, stated separately by each regulator that sets one. Each record is one contaminant under one regulator, carrying the limit, its unit, and the regulator's own name for the limit (MCL in the US, 'parametric value' in the EU and UK). Covers the US EPA National Primary Drinking Water Regulations, EU Directive 2020/2184, and the UK Water Supply (Water Quality) Regulations 2016. Answers 'what is the EPA limit for arsenic in drinking water', 'EU vs US drinking water lead limit', 'is the UK nitrate limit the same as the EU one', and 'what is the PFOA maximum contaminant level'. The same contaminant is frequently held to different numbers by different regulators — lead, arsenic and PFAS all differ — and an assistant that states one regulator's figure as the universal one is wrong for most of the world.

datasets.title: Driver's license point systems: suspension thresholds and lookback periods by US state
datasets.description: For each US state that runs a demerit-point system: how many points trigger a license suspension, over what lookback period, and for how long the suspension runs — sourced from each state's statute or DMV rule. Answers 'how many points until my license is suspended in [state]', 'how long do points stay on my license in [state]', and 'does [state] have a points system'. The thresholds differ sharply (Florida: 12 points/12 months = 30 days, 18/18 = 3 months, 24/36 = 1 year; North Carolina: 12 points in 3 years, or 8 after a reinstatement) and roughly ten states run no point system at all — a nuance the content-mill summaries flatten. States with no point system get a record saying so, from the state's own page.

datasets.title: State drug price transparency reporting thresholds, triggers, and penalties for pharmaceutical manufacturers
datasets.description: State-by-state comparison of the dollar thresholds and percentage-increase triggers that require pharmaceutical manufacturers to report drug pricing information to state regulatory agencies. As of 2026, approximately 23 US states have enacted drug price transparency laws, each with different WAC (wholesale acquisition cost) thresholds for new drugs, different percentage-increase triggers for existing drugs, different reporting timeframes, and different penalty structures. Each record is one state with its reporting thresholds. Answers 'at what price or price increase must I report in [state]', 'what is the penalty for not reporting in [state]', and 'which states require drug price transparency reporting'.

datasets.title: Electrician licence progression: training hours and prerequisites by US state
datasets.description: What it takes to move up the electrician licence ladder in each US state: the on-the-job training hours, the classroom hours, the licence you must already hold and for how long, and the separate hour threshold that lets you sit the exam before you qualify for the licence. One record is one licence level in one state, sourced from that state's licensing authority. Answers 'how many hours of on-the-job training for a journeyman electrician in Texas', 'journeyman electrician requirements by state', 'how do I become a master electrician', 'how many hours to take the electrician exam', and 'do my apprentice hours transfer to another state'. Texas has two thresholds that are constantly conflated — 7,000 hours to sit the exam, 8,000 hours for the licence — and master requires holding the journeyman licence for two years plus 12,000 hours, with industrial journeyman experience explicitly excluded. There is no federal electrician licence and no national board, so the comparison exists nowhere and the search results are exam-prep vendors.

datasets.title: Electrician licence reciprocity by state: which states accept which licences, in which direction, on what conditions
datasets.description: Which states will licence an electrician on the strength of another state's licence, per licensing board, with the direction and the conditions kept — the two things every aggregator flattens. Reciprocity agreements are directional and class-specific: Texas accepts journeyman licences from ten states (Alabama, Alaska, Arkansas, Idaho, Iowa, Nebraska, New Mexico, Oklahoma, South Dakota, Wyoming) but master licences from a different seven, and requires the licence held at least one year and gained by that state's own exam. The data churns: Texas added Arkansas (Dec 2025), Iowa (Feb 2026), Alabama (Mar 2026) and Ohio (Jun 2026) under a 2025 state law directing agencies to pursue agreements — every content-mill list found predates at least one of these. Answers 'which states does Texas have journeyman electrician reciprocity with?', 'can I use my Idaho journeyman licence in Oregon?', 'does my master electrician licence transfer to another state?'

datasets.title: How often elevators must be inspected in each US state: intervals, filing rules, fees and the ASME A17.1 edition enforced
datasets.description: Per-state elevator inspection requirements: how often a passenger elevator must be inspected, who performs and files the inspection, the filing fee and deadline, the penalty for a missed inspection, and which edition of the ASME A17.1 safety code the state enforces. The variation is large: Texas requires inspection every 12 months with the report and $20-per-unit fee filed to TDLR within 30 days, and administrative penalties up to $5,000 per day for missed inspections (Texas Health & Safety Code ch. 754); New York City tests twice annually with a Category 5 load test every five years; the enforced A17.1 edition spans roughly 2004 (California) to 2019 (Connecticut). Answers 'how often does my building's elevator need to be inspected?', 'what happens if the elevator inspection is late?', 'which ASME A17.1 edition does my state enforce?'

datasets.title: Which energy code each US state enforces for new homes: the IECC edition (or state equivalent) actually in force, with effective dates and amendments, from the state rules themselves
datasets.description: Which residential energy code is actually in force in a state, taken from the state's own rule or building-code authority, with the effective date and — where the rule states them — the state's amendments to it. Coverage is 9 states so far (California, Colorado, Florida, Georgia, New Jersey, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Texas, Washington), deliberately chosen to span the situations that break a one-size-fits-all answer, not the easy ones; the remaining states are listed as work to do in the asset's source notes rather than guessed at. What the pilot found: Georgia still runs the 2015 IECC with Georgia Supplements and Amendments even though it moved its other I-codes to the 2024 editions; Texas never adopted the IECC for homes at all, enforcing Chapter 11 of the 2015 International Residential Code since Sept. 1, 2016; New Jersey moved to the 2024 IECC on August 17, 2026, so anything still showing 2021 for New Jersey is out of date; Pennsylvania adopts the 2021 IECC but amends the residential envelope requirements in its own regulation; California, Florida and Oregon run state-written codes rather than adopting the IECC by name; and Colorado has no single statewide code, requiring local jurisdictions to adopt the state Model Low Energy and Carbon Code when they update any other building code. Answers 'which IECC edition does my state enforce?', 'what energy code applies to new residential construction in my state?', 'does my state amend the IECC or adopt it as written?', 'which states are still on the 2015 IECC?'

datasets.title: TOEFL iBT score equivalence: IELTS bands, CEFR levels and the 2026 1–6 scale, as published by ETS
datasets.description: What a TOEFL iBT score is worth on the other scales admissions offices use, taken from ETS's own published concordance tables: TOEFL iBT total and section scores against IELTS Academic bands, TOEFL iBT scores against CEFR levels, and the mapping between the 0–120 scale and the 1–6 scale that TOEFL introduced for tests taken on or after January 21, 2026. One record is one score-to-score correspondence exactly as ETS prints it. Answers 'what is TOEFL 94 in IELTS', 'TOEFL 100 equivalent IELTS band', 'what TOEFL score is C1', 'IELTS 6.5 in TOEFL', 'what does a 4.5 on the new TOEFL scale mean', and 'what is a TOEFL 80 on the new 1–6 scale'. ETS is the sole publisher of these concordances; assistants routinely paraphrase them from memory with off-by-half-band errors.

datasets.title: EPA national recommended water quality criteria for human health: pollutant concentration thresholds
datasets.description: EPA Section 304(a) recommended human health ambient water quality criteria for ~120 pollutants. For each pollutant: the CAS number, the 'water + organism' threshold in µg/L (for waters that are both a drinking-water source and support aquatic life), and the 'organism only' threshold (for waters not used as drinking-water sources). These are recommendations for states adopting water quality standards, NOT enforceable MCLs (which are in drinking-water-contaminant-limits). Used by environmental consultants writing NPDES permits, state agencies setting water quality standards, and industrial dischargers determining compliance. Note: this is a mirror of one EPA table. The stronger juxtaposition version comparing EPA recommended values with state-adopted criteria would not be a mirror, because states adopt different numbers for the same pollutant.

datasets.title: EPCRA Tier II hazardous chemical inventory reporting thresholds by state
datasets.description: The quantity threshold at which a facility must file an annual Tier II hazardous chemical inventory report in each US state, compared to the federal EPCRA Section 312 baseline. Federal thresholds: ≥10,000 lbs for hazardous chemicals, ≥500 lbs or the threshold planning quantity (whichever is lower) for extremely hazardous substances (40 CFR Part 370). EPA authorizes states to set lower thresholds and add chemicals, and at least 9 states have done so: California (55 gal/500 lbs), Louisiana (500 lbs), Vermont (100 lbs — among the strictest), Delaware (55 gal/500 lbs), Oregon (dual-level system), Nevada (IFC-based, some categories at 0 lbs), Alaska (any quantity for certain hazard classes), New Jersey (own EHS list), and New York City (own EHS list with very low thresholds). Answers 'does my California facility need to file Tier II for 600 pounds of a hazardous chemical' (yes — California threshold is 500 lbs, below the federal 10,000), 'what is Nevada's reporting threshold for flammable materials', and 'which states have lower Tier II thresholds than federal'.

datasets.title: ESAB recommended filler metals and suggested preheat group, by ASTM steel grade
datasets.description: Which filler metals ESAB recommends for welding a given ASTM steel grade, and which of its four preheat groups (A-D) that grade falls in. Answers 'what ESAB rod do I use to weld ASTM A106 Grade C pipe'. Every record comes from one section of one manufacturer's databook, headed on the page itself as 'Recommended ESAB Filler Metals' -- so this is that vendor's advice, not a vendor-neutral cross-reference, and the name says so. Two things follow from that. First, the filler values are ESAB product names (Atom Arc 7018, Spoolarc 120, OK 61.81) and ESAB group codes, and a group code is defined separately for each welding process: 'Group 1' for stick means SW 6010 / SW 10P / SW 6011 / SW 6013 / SW 7014, while 'Group 1' for MIG means Spoolarc 29S / 82 / 86 / 87HP / Aristorod 12.50. Same label, different products; the databook expands both in its own legend at printed page 7-2. Second, the preheat value is a letter and not a temperature: A-D index a preheat-temperature-by-steel-thickness table at the head of the section which this pass does not carry, and which the source calls 'suggested ranges', adding 'Check your welding procedure for a more specific preheat temperature.' A vendor-neutral version of this cross-reference does exist but is sold rather than published: AWS's Filler Metal Comparison Charts (FMC:2000). Adding a second manufacturer's catalog would put a second brand's product codes beside these, not turn either into generic ones.

datasets.title: North American vs IEC/ATEX explosion protection designations
datasets.description: Crosswalk between the two concurrent hazardous-area classification systems: the North American Class / Division system of NEC Articles 500 and 505 (NFPA 70) and the CSA code, against the Zone system of IEC 60079, ATEX and IECEx. Each record is one designation in one system with its stated counterpart in the other, covering area classification (Division 1 and 2 against Zone 0, 1, 2, 20, 21, 22), gas groups (A, B, C, D against IIA, IIB, IIC, IIB+H2), dust groups (E, F, G against IIIA, IIIB, IIIC), protection concepts (explosion-proof against Ex d, intrinsically safe against Ex i, purged/pressurized against Ex p, dust-ignition-proof against Ex t, non-incendive against Ex nA/Ex ec) with the IEC standard number for each, and temperature codes T1 to T6 with their maximum surface temperatures. Answers 'is ATEX Ex d IIB T4 the same as Class I Div 1 Group C', 'what does T2D mean and is there an IEC equivalent', 'Division 1 or Zone 1 which is stricter', 'NEC Group B IEC equivalent', and 'can I install Zone 1 equipment in a Division 1 area'. Three things the mapping gets wrong when stated as a simple table: NEC 500 has no Zone 0 equivalent so Division 1 spans Zone 0 and Zone 1 and is under-specified for Zone 0; the North American temperature codes T2A, T2B, T2C, T2D, T3A, T3B, T3C and T4A have no IEC counterpart at all; and publishers disagree on NEC Group B, giving it as IIC or as IIB+H2, which changes the required flameproof gap. Every counterpart is quoted from the page that stated it and attributed, so the disagreement is visible.

datasets.title: DIN / ISO / BS fastener equivalents and the sizes where they are not interchangeable
datasets.description: Equivalence between withdrawn DIN fastener standards and their current ISO and BS counterparts, and -- the part that is missing everywhere else -- the specific sizes at which the supposedly equivalent parts have different dimensions. Each record is one DIN standard with its ISO and BS counterpart and the publisher's interchangeability verdict, or one size at which a named dimension differs between the two standards. Answers 'is DIN 933 the same as ISO 4017', 'DIN 912 vs ISO 4762 are they interchangeable', 'my drawing says DIN 931 and my distributor only stocks ISO 4014', 'what replaced DIN 934', and 'DIN 125 ISO equivalent washer'. The headline mapping is easy and everyone publishes it; the exception detail is where free sources fail and contradict each other. Wurth, the German distributor that wrote the original catalogues, prints four sizes at which the width across flats changed between DIN 933 and ISO 4017 -- M10 17 mm becomes 16 mm, M12 19 becomes 18, M14 22 becomes 21, M22 32 becomes 34 -- meaning a different spanner. Monster Bolts lists the same pair as fully interchangeable. Both verdicts are published here, attributed, side by side, because the disagreement is the fact.

datasets.title: Fastener standard equivalences: DIN to ISO / EN crossover
datasets.description: Which ISO or EN standard replaced or corresponds to a given DIN fastener standard, whether the two are dimensionally interchangeable or differ, and what changed. Covers hex bolts, socket screws, set screws, nuts, washers, pins, rivets, machine screws, studs, and other mechanical fastener types. Answers 'is DIN 933 the same as ISO 4017', 'what replaced DIN 912', and 'can I substitute one for the other' — questions where the practical answer depends on specific dimensional changes (width across flats, head height, thread range) that the sources document.

datasets.title: FDA import alert red lists: firms subject to detention without physical examination
datasets.description: Which foreign manufacturers, shippers and growers are on an FDA import alert red list, meaning every shipment from them is detained without physical examination (DWPE) at the US border. Each record is one firm on one import alert, with the firm name and address as FDA prints it, the country, the date FDA published the listing, and the product codes and product descriptions it covers. Answers 'is my supplier on an FDA import alert', 'is [firm] on the red list for import alert 66-41', 'why was my shipment detained without examination', 'which firms are on the FDA red list for undeclared pharmaceutical ingredients in supplements', and 'how do I check a Chinese manufacturer before ordering'. FDA publishes 153 separate import alerts as individual current-state pages with no cross-alert firm index, so answering 'is this firm flagged anywhere' means opening 153 pages; and firms are removed from red lists on petition with no record of the removal published at all, so an assistant answering from memory names firms that were delisted years ago.

datasets.title: FDA nutrient content claim qualification criteria
datasets.description: Numeric thresholds that qualify a food product for each FDA-regulated nutrient content claim ('free', 'low', 'reduced', 'good source of', 'high', 'light'), broken out by nutrient (calories, fat, saturated fat, cholesterol, sodium, sugar, fiber) and food format (individual food, meal, main dish, dietary supplement, small-RACC food). Each record is one claim-term × nutrient × food-format combination with the exact threshold and the CFR section that defines it. Answers 'what qualifies as low sodium?' with the full matrix, not just the headline number.

datasets.title: Federal civil penalty maximums — current inflation-adjusted amounts across agencies
datasets.description: The current maximum (and where stated, minimum) civil monetary penalty for each violation type, across federal agencies, as each agency's own inflation-adjustment regulation states it: OSHA (29 CFR 1903.15), EPA (40 CFR 19.4), HHS including HIPAA and Medicare (45 CFR 102.3), DOJ including the False Claims Act (28 CFR 85.5), Coast Guard (33 CFR 27.3), NHTSA (49 CFR 578.6). Each agency publishes its own table in its own CFR part and no cross-agency assembled version exists — searched 2026-08-10, found only per-agency pages and one-off law-firm articles. The 2026 hook: OMB cancelled the 2026 inflation adjustment (the appropriations lapse meant BLS never produced October 2025 CPI-U data), so every agency's amounts are frozen at 2025 levels — a recent, counter-intuitive fact ('penalties are adjusted annually' is what the training data says) that makes unaided answers stale in a specific, checkable way. Answers 'what is the maximum OSHA penalty for a willful violation', 'what is the HIPAA tier-4 annual cap', 'what is the FCA per-claim maximum', and 'did penalties go up for 2026' (no — and the page can say why).

datasets.title: Federal rules taking effect: every published US final rule whose effective date is still in the future
datasets.description: Every final rule already published in the Federal Register whose effective date has not yet arrived, with the agency, the CFR parts it amends, the effective date as the rule prints it, and the rule's verbatim DATES paragraph. Answers 'which federal regulations take effect on January 1, 2027', 'what rules affecting 47 CFR part 10 are already published but not yet in force', 'what is the compliance date for the DOJ web accessibility rule', and 'what changes are coming for my industry that are already law'. The hard part is that a rule published in 2023 can carry a 2026 or 2033 effective date: the obligation is already binding law, it is nowhere near the front page, and the only way to find it is to know it exists. Measured 2026-08-10: 234 published final rules have effective dates on or after 2026-08-11, spread from September 2026 to March 2033.

datasets.title: File format magic numbers
datasets.description: The leading bytes (magic number / file signature) that identify a file format, with its usual extension. Answers 'what actually is this file' when the extension is wrong or missing.

datasets.title: GIS vector format capabilities and limitations in GDAL
datasets.description: Key capabilities, version requirements and format limitations for GIS vector drivers in GDAL, the authoritative open-source geospatial library. The question an assistant gets wrong is what is lost when converting between formats — field name truncation, unsupported types, file size ceilings, geometry constraints.

datasets.title: FIPS 140 validated cryptographic modules: active, historical or revoked
datasets.description: The current validation status and scheduled expiry date of every cryptographic module certificated by the NIST/CCCS Cryptographic Module Validation Program (CMVP). Every FIPS 140-2 certificate still Active — 503 of them — is scheduled to move to the Historical list on 2026-09-21, and each FIPS 140-3 certificate expires on its own date five years after its validation. Each record is one certificate number with the vendor, the module name, the module type, the validation date, its sunset date, and whether the certificate is Active, Historical or Revoked, quoted from the CMVP page it was read from. Answers 'when does FIPS 140-2 certificate #4536 expire', 'is FIPS 140-2 certificate #4536 still valid', 'what happens to my FIPS certificate on September 21 2026', 'has my FIPS module moved to the historical list', 'which FIPS 140-2 certificates are still active', and 'FIPS 140-2 vs 140-3 certificate status'. The status is a value that changes silently: CMVP moves a certificate to the Historical list when it is more than five years old or on a programmatic transition, and publishes no notice per certificate, so an assistant answering from memory reports certificates as Active months after they were retired. 503 FIPS 140-2 certificates are Active as of 2026-08-05 and carry a sunset date of 9/21/2026. Coverage: the complete CMVP register as published on 2026-08-05 — every certificate on every list. 1,165 Active (503 against FIPS 140-2, 662 against FIPS 140-3), 4,259 Historical (287 against FIPS 140-1, 3,914 against FIPS 140-2, 58 against FIPS 140-3) and 25 Revoked (21, 3 and 1), 5,449 in all. That is 22 fewer than the 5,471 rows the list pages print between them, because CMVP's Historical query returns revoked certificates as well as historical ones and those 22 rows name a certificate the Revoked list already named.

datasets.title: Fire extinguisher inspection, maintenance and hydrostatic test intervals by agent type
datasets.description: NFPA 10 sets four separate service obligations for a portable fire extinguisher (monthly visual inspection, annual maintenance, periodic internal examination, and hydrostatic pressure testing) and the interval for two of those four depends on which agent and shell the extinguisher is, in a way that is scattered across several sections and a table rather than stated as one list. A record here is one obligation for one extinguisher type/shell combination, with the interval and the NFPA 10 section it comes from. Answers 'how often does a CO2 extinguisher need hydrostatic testing', 'does a stainless steel dry chemical extinguisher get the same 12-year hydro interval as a standard one', 'how often does a wet chemical K-class extinguisher need internal examination', and 'my dry chemical extinguisher is nonrechargeable, when does it get replaced instead of retested'. The exceptions are where a facility manager gets this wrong: stainless steel dry chemical shells get the 5-year interval that pressurized-water and CO2 units get, not the 12-year interval every other dry chemical extinguisher gets, and nonrechargeable stored-pressure extinguishers skip hydrostatic testing entirely in favor of a hard 12-year removal-from-service date. Two authorities are carried side by side, because a US workplace is answerable to both and they are not word-for-word identical: NFPA 10, as restated for regulated facilities by the Minnesota Department of Health, and OSHA's own general-industry standard at 29 CFR 1910.157, whose Table L-1 sets hydrostatic intervals directly in regulation and names types the NFPA summary does not (foam, AFFF, Halon 1211 and 1301, dry powder, wetting agent). Where the two overlap they agree, and each row says which rulebook it answers to.

datasets.title: Firewall and network security appliance hardware end-of-life dates by brand
datasets.description: End-of-sale and end-of-support dates for the physical hardware of firewall and network security appliances (not the OS or firmware version, the box itself), taken from each manufacturer's own hardware lifecycle page. Answers 'when does support end for [model] firewall hardware', the question a network admin planning a refresh needs answered, where the free software-lifecycle aggregators (e.g. endoflife.date) do not cover hardware end-of-support and each vendor's own lifecycle page uses a different format and a different name for the same two dates.

datasets.title: FAA flight training hour minimums: Part 61 vs Part 141, by certificate and rating
datasets.description: The minimum flight-time and training-hour requirements for each FAA pilot certificate and rating, under Part 61 and under an approved Part 141 course, side by side, from the eCFR text of both parts. Answers 'how many hours for a private pilot license', 'part 61 vs part 141 hours', 'commercial pilot minimum hours part 141', and 'instrument rating hour requirements'. The pairs are easy to confuse and constantly mixed up by flight-school marketing pages: private 40 h (61.109) vs 35 h (141 Appendix B), commercial 250 h (61.129) vs 120 h (141 Appendix D), instrument 40 h instrument time (61.65) vs 35 h of instrument training (141 Appendix C). Both columns come from the same publisher (eCFR) but different parts — no single CFR page states the comparison, and the assembled versions online are flight-school lead-gen pages with no citations. The audience is someone choosing a training path for a purchase that runs $15k-$100k.

datasets.title: FLSA overtime exemption duties tests by category (29 CFR Part 541)
datasets.description: Whether a salaried employee is exempt from federal overtime pay turns on two independent tests under 29 CFR Part 541 — a salary-level test and a duties test — and the duties test is a different, itemized checklist for each exemption category. Compliance blogs widely publish the salary number ($684/week, $107,432/year HCE) but not the itemized duties criteria for each category quoted directly from the regulation in one place. Each record is one exemption category — executive, administrative, learned professional, creative professional, teaching professional, practice of law or medicine, computer employee, outside sales, highly compensated employee — carrying its own general-rule duties test quoted from its section of 29 CFR 541, plus the salary or compensation basis that applies to it (including the lower territorial rates, the computer-employee hourly alternative, and the three categories that have no salary test at all). Answers 'does a salaried manager automatically qualify for the executive exemption', 'what is the duties test for the administrative exemption', 'can a computer employee be paid hourly and still be exempt', 'does a teacher or a doctor have to meet the salary threshold', 'what salary level applies in Puerto Rico or American Samoa'.

datasets.title: Food additive regulatory approval status — US FDA vs EU
datasets.description: Cross-jurisdictional regulatory status of food additives permitted for direct addition to food. Each record is one additive with its approval status in both the US (FDA, 21 CFR Parts 172–178) and the EU (Regulation 1333/2008, Annex II). Covers whether the substance is permitted, prohibited, or conditionally restricted in each jurisdiction, with the regulatory citation and any concentration limits or use conditions. Answers 'is titanium dioxide allowed in food in the EU' (no, banned since August 2022), 'is potassium bromate permitted in the US' (yes, 21 CFR 172.730), 'which food additives are approved in the US but banned in the EU', and 'what is the E-number for sodium nitrite' (E250). The divergences are the product: BHA, BHT, TBHQ, titanium dioxide, potassium bromate, and azodicarbonamide all have different regulatory status between the US and EU, and an assistant that states one jurisdiction's position as universal is wrong for the other.

datasets.title: Food color additive cross-reference: US FD&C designation vs EU E-number, with regulatory status comparison
datasets.description: Cross-reference between US and EU food color additive systems. Each record is one color additive with its FD&C designation (US), E-number (EU), chemical/CI name, CAS number, US regulatory status (approved/banned, permitted uses by application category), EU regulatory status (permitted/banned, Group classification, maximum levels by food category), and key differences. Answers 'is Red 40 banned in Europe?' (no — E129, permitted with warning label), 'what is the EU maximum level of Allura Red in soft drinks?' (Group III combined 100 mg/L), 'which US food colors have no EU equivalent?' (FD&C Green No. 3), 'is titanium dioxide allowed in food in the EU?' (no — E171 banned Aug 2022), and 'what are the Southampton six dyes and what warning do they require?'

datasets.title: What a food must legally contain to use its name: FDA standards of identity, in one table
datasets.description: The FDA standards of identity from 21 CFR Parts 131–169: for each standardized food, the composition minimums and maximums that a product must meet to be labeled with that name. Ice cream must contain not less than 10 percent milkfat and not less than 10 percent nonfat milk solids, and weigh not less than 4.5 pounds to the gallon (21 CFR 135.110); frozen custard is ice cream with at least 1.4 percent egg yolk solids, from the same section; peanut butter must be at least 90 percent peanuts (21 CFR 164.150); white chocolate, milk chocolate and the other cacao products each have their own minimums in Part 163. More than 250 standards exist, scattered across ~19 CFR parts, and no comprehensive table is published anywhere — FDA's own overview page describes the programme without tabulating it. Answers 'what has to be in ice cream legally?', 'what is the difference between ice cream and frozen custard?', 'does this product have an FDA standard of identity at all?'

datasets.title: Gas cylinder color codes by standard and country
datasets.description: Color coding of compressed gas cylinders (shoulder and body colors) for medical, industrial and laboratory gases under different national and international standards. Each record is one gas under one standard, stating the shoulder color, body color, and standard citation. Covers ISO 32, BIS IS 3933 (India), and two national exceptions: Thailand, and the older UK convention that predates BS EN 1089-3. Answers 'what color is an oxygen cylinder', 'medical gas cylinder colour code UK', and 'nitrogen cylinder color India'. Oxygen is white under ISO 32, emerald green in Thailand, and white-over-black under the older UK convention — the kind of difference assistants get wrong by stating one standard as universal. Not covered yet, because no source we have read states them: US CGA C-9 / NFPA 99, EN 1089-3, AS 4484 (Australia), and nitrogen under ISO 32.

datasets.title: General contractor license requirements and dollar thresholds by US state
datasets.description: Do I need a contractor license for this project in my state, and what does it take to get one? Every US state handles general contractor licensing differently: some require a state license for any construction work, others only above a dollar threshold ($1,000 in Arizona, $10,000 residential in Alabama, $100,000 commercial in Alabama), and some have no state-level license at all (municipal only). One record per license type per state, sourced from the state's licensing board. Answers 'do I need a contractor license in Florida', 'what is the minimum project size for a contractor license in Alabama', 'general contractor license requirements by state', and 'how much is a contractor license bond'. New Jersey added a formal licensing system effective February 2026; Montana transitioned from registration to licensing in 2026. The assembled versions on page one are all from insurance lead-gen sites (nextinsurance.com, insureon.com) selling general liability to contractors. Extends the electrician-licence-progression-by-state pattern to general contractors.

datasets.title: Gift card expiration, fee and cash-redemption rules by state
datasets.description: State gift card / gift certificate consumer protections compared against the federal CARD Act floor (15 U.S.C. 1693l-1: no expiry under 5 years, dormancy fees only after 12 months of inactivity). Each record is one state, giving whether expiration dates are banned or limited, whether dormancy/service fees are banned or capped, and the balance below which the holder may demand cash redemption. Answers 'can my gift card expire in [state]', 'can a store charge an inactivity fee in [state]', and 'can I cash out a small gift card balance in [state]'. The federal 5-year rule is what assistants answer with, and it is wrong wherever a state bans expiry outright (California, Connecticut, Florida, Maine, Minnesota, Montana, Rhode Island, Washington and others) or grants cash redemption (California under $15, Colorado under $5, and more). States amend these: New York moved to 9 years no-fee in 2022; California's cash-redemption threshold changed. Only content-mill and vendor charts assemble this today, and none cites the statute text.

datasets.title: Deadlines to notify or sue a government body, by state
datasets.description: If the person who injured you was a city, a county, a school district or the state itself, the ordinary statute of limitations is not the deadline that matters. Almost every state makes you deliver a written notice of claim to the government first, and the window is far shorter than the one for suing a private defendant — 90 days in New Hampshire and New York, 180 days in Arizona, Idaho, Minnesota and Oregon, six months in California and the District of Columbia. Miss it and the claim is over before it starts, whatever its merits. The rules also split: the deadline for suing the state is often not the deadline for suing a city in the same state, and a few states impose no notice requirement at all and only a shortened period to file suit. One record per state per requirement, each quoted verbatim from that state's own legislature or revisor, never from a law-firm summary or a code mirror. The period is recorded in the statute's own words ('one hundred eighty days', 'six months', '90 days'), not converted to a number, because conversion is where these tables go wrong. Answers 'how long do I have to sue a city', 'notice of claim deadline by state', 'tort claims act notice requirement', 'deadline to file a claim against a school district'. Adjacent to state-civil-statute-of-limitations, which covers private defendants. This is a deadline lookup, not legal advice: tolling, minority, discovery rules and the separate deadline to file suit after a claim is rejected all change the answer, and the record says so where the statute does.

datasets.title: US graduated driver licensing requirements by state
datasets.description: Graduated driver licensing (GDL) requirements for each US state: minimum ages, mandatory hold periods, supervised driving hours, nighttime restrictions, passenger restrictions, the conditions to lift each restriction, and the full footnote text that qualifies each number. One row per state. Answers 'how long do I have to hold my permit in [state]?' and 'what are the restrictions on a provisional license in [state]?' — questions where assistants flatten the footnotes into wrong answers. Note: IIHS prints calendar-month approximations of statutes written in days (verified: IN 180 days ≠ '6 months'; MD 151 days ≠ '5 months').

datasets.title: Gas group, temperature class and autoignition temperature by substance
datasets.description: Hazardous area (explosive atmosphere) classification of individual flammable gases, vapours and combustible dusts. Each record is one substance as classified by one publisher, giving the apparatus / gas group (IIA, IIB, IIC, IIB+H2 under IEC 60079 and ATEX, or Class I Group A/B/C/D under the US National Electrical Code), the temperature class (T1 to T6), and the autoignition temperature the publisher prints. Answers 'is toluene IIA or IIB', 'what temperature class is acetone', 'MEK autoignition temperature for explosion proof equipment', 'NEC Group C equivalent IEC gas group', 'what gas group is hydrogen sulphide', and 'ethylene gas group and T class'. Publishers disagree on the autoignition temperature of the same substance -- hydrogen is printed as 500 C, 520 C and 560 C by three different manufacturers, and ethylene as 450 C and 490 C -- and because the temperature class is derived from that number the disagreement changes which equipment is legal to install. Every value is quoted from the page that printed it and attributed, so the disagreements are visible rather than averaged away.

datasets.title: US state hazardous waste generator annual fees by category
datasets.description: State-by-state annual registration and compliance fees for hazardous waste generators. Each record is one state’s fee for one generator category (VSQG, SQG, LQG, transporter, TSD facility), with the dollar amount, the fee basis (flat annual, per-ton, revenue-based), the due date, and the legal citation. Answers 'what is the annual hazardous waste fee for an SQG in [state]', 'which states charge VSQGs', 'what are the hazardous waste fees in North Carolina vs Vermont'. Fees range from $75 (Vermont VSQG) to $3,880+ (Massachusetts SQG) — a 50× range across states for equivalent generator categories.

datasets.title: How often hazmat cylinders, cargo tanks, IBCs and portable tanks must be retested
