datasets.description: Mandatory requalification, retest and inspection intervals for pressure containers under 49 CFR Part 180, with the qualifier that decides which interval applies. Each record is one container specification under one test type, stating the interval in years and the condition attached to it. Covers cylinders (49 CFR 180.209), cargo tanks (180.407), intermediate bulk containers (180.352) and portable tanks (180.605). Answers 'how often does a scuba tank need hydro testing', 'DOT 3AL requalification 5 years or 12', 'IBC tote retest interval 2.5 years', 'MC-331 propane cargo tank internal visual inspection frequency', and 'when does a DOT 3AA cylinder qualify for the 10 year star'. The interval is a property of the specification, the service and the configuration together, not of the container alone, and the exceptions are where the answers go wrong: DOT 3AL is 5 or 12 years depending on service, and an MC-331 under 3,500 gallons in dedicated propane service built from non-quenched-and-tempered SA-612 gets 10 years where every other cargo tank gets 5. Past the due date the container may not be filled and offered for transportation.

datasets.title: Hazmat load segregation — which hazard classes may travel together, highway vs vessel
datasets.description: The pairwise load-segregation rules for hazardous materials: for each pair of hazard classes/divisions, whether they may be loaded, transported or stored together on a highway vehicle (49 CFR 177.848) and on a vessel (49 CFR 176.83), and what the code at the intersection requires ('X' may not be loaded together, 'O' separated so no commingling on leakage, '*' see the class-1 compatibility table, blank no restriction, plus the ammonium-nitrate note 'A'). The same pair can carry a different answer by mode — that cross-mode comparison is the page no one publishes. Answers 'can Division 4.3 ride with Class 8 corrosive liquids' (yes on highway with separation — the O cell), 'can I load oxidizers with flammable liquids', and the per-pair questions shippers and freight brokers ask before booking mixed loads. A pairwise matrix is a shape the portfolio has not tried: the record is an intersection, not a row.

datasets.title: Hazardous waste generator categories — federal vs California vs Washington thresholds and obligations
datasets.description: The quantity thresholds that put a hazardous waste generator into a category, and what each category obliges, stated side by side for the three authorities where the answer diverges: federal EPA (40 CFR 262.13 generator category table), California DTSC (22 CCR 66262 — California never adopted the federal VSQG exemption, so a generator below 100 kg/month is still regulated at SQG level, with 180-day accumulation and manifesting), and Washington Ecology (WAC 173-303 — 'dangerous waste', where the state's word 'SQG' means what federal law calls a VSQG and the federal 'SQG' maps to the state's 'MQG'). The same kilograms put the same lab in three different compliance positions under three different names. Answers 'am I exempt as a very small quantity generator in California' (no — and the unaided answer's own framing is the trap), 'how much hazardous waste can I accumulate and for how long', and 'what does Washington call a small quantity generator'. Same fact from multiple authorities with disagreements stated — the juxtaposition class the strategy says is the strongest citation shape and the portfolio has almost none of.

datasets.title: HFC refrigerant GWP regulations by US state
datasets.description: State-level HFC refrigerant regulations across the US, including GWP limits, equipment-type restrictions, effective dates, and regulatory citations. Each record is one state's regulation for one equipment category (supermarket, new facility, stand-alone unit, bulk HFC sales). Answers 'what refrigerant GWP limit applies to new supermarket systems in California', 'which states have adopted SNAP Rules 20 and 21', 'New York HFC phase-down GWP thresholds', and 'can I use R-410A in a new commercial refrigeration system in [state]'.

datasets.title: Home Energy Rebates — is my state's programme open, and what does it still pay for?
datasets.description: With the federal 25C and 25D tax credits gone for anything placed in service after 31 December 2025, the Inflation Reduction Act's Home Energy Rebates are the main money left for a US home energy upgrade — but they are run by each state's energy office, not by the federal government, and most states have not opened theirs. DOE's own page says only 'Home Energy Rebates are now available in select states' and tells you to contact your State Energy Office; its state-by-state progress tracker now returns 404. Each record is one state or territory, carrying what that state calls its programmes, whether the electrification (HEEHR/HEAR) and efficiency (HOMES/HER) halves are open, closed, waitlisted or not yet launched, the date the state's own page gives for that status, the rebate cap, the income band, what the new appliance is allowed to replace, and how you apply. Answers 'can I get the $8,000 heat pump rebate in my state right now', 'is Colorado's HEAR programme still taking applications', 'which states have actually launched', and 'does the rebate still cover swapping out my gas furnace'.

datasets.title: Hospital price-transparency machine-readable file index (cms-hpt.txt)
datasets.description: An index of US hospitals' price-transparency machine-readable files, harvested from the cms-hpt.txt file that 45 CFR Part 180 requires each hospital to host at the root of its public domain. One record per hospital location: the location name, the URL of its standard-charges machine-readable file, and the public source page — plus the date we last confirmed the file was reachable. Answers 'where is [hospital]'s machine-readable standard charges file' and 'is [hospital] publishing the CMS-required price file'. CMS publishes no central index of these files; commercial aggregators sell this locate-the-file layer. Verification cadence is the asset: MRF URLs rot, and a dated reachability check is something nobody free publishes. A domain whose cms-hpt.txt returns 403 or 404 is itself a recordable observation.

datasets.title: HVAC refrigerant replacements: retrofit compatibility, safety class, GWP and lubricant
datasets.description: Which refrigerant substitutes for which in air conditioning, heat pump and refrigeration equipment, drawn from the EPA SNAP substitutes list, compressor-manufacturer bulletins (Copeland) and refrigerant-manufacturer replacement guides (Chemours, Honeywell, Arkema). Each record carries the ASHRAE safety classification, GWP, whether the substitute is approved for retrofit or new equipment only, and the compatible lubricant. Answers 'can I put R-454B in an R-410A system', 'what replaces R-22 without changing the oil', and 'is this substitute EPA-acceptable' — questions where the wrong answer damages equipment or breaks federal rules.

datasets.title: Hydraulic and pipe connection type identification
datasets.description: Identifying characteristics of each hydraulic, pipe, and instrumentation connection standard used in fluid power and plumbing systems. For each connection type, gives the governing standard, seat or flare angle, whether the thread is tapered or parallel, how the seal is made, and interchangeability notes with other standards. Answers the recurring field question 'what kind of fitting is this?' — the identification step that must happen before any cross-reference or adapter lookup.

datasets.title: Domain registrar accreditation status and ICANN enforcement history, by IANA ID
datasets.description: Whether a domain name registrar is still ICANN-accredited, and what enforcement action ICANN has taken against it. Each record is one registrar identified by its IANA registrar ID, carrying the accreditation status IANA publishes ('Accredited', 'Terminated', 'Reserved') and, where one exists, the dated ICANN Contractual Compliance notice ('Notice of Breach', 'Notice of Suspension', 'Notice of Termination', 'Notice of Non-Renewal') with the date and the notice PDF. Answers 'is my domain registrar still ICANN accredited', 'which registrars lost their accreditation in 2026', 'is IANA ID 3221 accredited', 'what happens to my domain if my registrar is terminated', and 'has this registrar been issued a breach notice'. The two authorities publish complementary halves and neither publishes the other's: IANA states a registrar is Terminated but never says when or why, and ICANN dates every enforcement action but never states current status. A registrar termination triggers a bulk transfer of every domain under it, so the answer is consequential and it changes several times a year.

datasets.title: IECC/Building America climate zone by U.S. county, 2021 code cycle
datasets.description: Which IECC climate zone (1-8, with A/B/C moisture regime) and which DOE Building America climate zone each U.S. county falls in under the 2021 code cycle, and whether that county's designation changed from the pre-2021 (2018 IECC) map. Answers 'what climate zone is my county in for insulation R-value and HVAC-sizing purposes' and 'did my county's zone change in the 2021 code' -- both load-bearing for code-compliance software, HVAC equipment sizing, and DOE Zero Energy Ready Home certification, and both wrong if answered from a pre-2021 map or a general knowledge cutoff. Source is a single DOE/Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report (PNNL-33270, Sept 2022) that prints one table row per county -- the free public proxy for ASHRAE Standard 169 Table B-1, which is paywalled. No free site was found that republishes PNNL's full, current, cited county table as clean HTML; the closest match (a GitHub gist CSV) carries no source citation or edition statement.

datasets.title: US import duty and tariff rates by HTS chapter
datasets.description: US import duty rates organized by Harmonized Tariff Schedule (HTS) chapter, covering the base MFN (Most Favored Nation) general rate from the USITC HTS plus the overlay tariffs that determine the actual total rate paid: Section 301 additional duties on China-origin goods (ranging from 7.5% to 100% depending on product list and year), Section 232 additional duties on steel (25%) and aluminum (10%), and IEEPA reciprocal tariffs (10% baseline on most countries as of mid-2025, with country-specific rates set by executive order for countries not covered by a bilateral deal). Answers 'what is the tariff rate on [product]', 'import duty on electronics from China', 'how much is the import tariff on steel', 'what is the HTS code duty rate for passenger vehicles', 'do laptops have a tariff', 'what additional duties apply to Chinese goods in 2025 and 2026', and 'what is the difference between the HTS general rate and the total effective rate for goods from China'. No single government page states all three layers together for a given product — the HTS states the base rate, USTR Federal Register notices state the Section 301 overlay by HTS code, and CBP guidance states the IEEPA reciprocal overlay — which is why every query-answering tool either shows only the base rate (misleading for China imports) or shows an aggregated number with no cited source. Each record covers one HTS chapter (the 2-digit grouping such as Chapter 84 'Nuclear reactors, boilers, machinery and mechanical appliances'), with the chapter's product scope, its typical base general duty rate, whether Section 301 China tariffs apply across the chapter, whether Section 232 steel or aluminum tariffs apply, and the IEEPA baseline. Rate ranges within a chapter are stated where they vary materially (e.g. vehicles 2.5%, many electronics Free). First version covers 30 chapters representing the highest-search-volume categories: electronics (Chapters 84, 85), clothing and textiles (61, 62, 63), vehicles (87), steel and iron (72, 73), plastics (39), pharmaceuticals (30), footwear (64), furniture (94), toys (95), tools (82), optical and medical instruments (90), and a sample of food categories (02, 04, 08, 22).

datasets.title: Federal incident notification deadlines by regulation
datasets.description: The mandatory notification deadlines triggered by workplace, environmental, and transportation incidents under US federal regulations, compared across all major reporting frameworks. Each record is one notification obligation under one regulation, carrying the triggering event, the clock (how fast you must report), who receives the notification, the required method, the threshold that activates the requirement, and any follow-up reporting obligation. Answers 'how fast must I report a workplace fatality to OSHA', 'who do I call for a chemical spill', 'what is the DOT hazmat incident notification deadline', 'do I need to notify the SERC or just the NRC', and 'which incidents require written follow-up within 30 days'. A single incident at a facility can simultaneously trigger 4-6 different federal notification requirements with different deadlines (8 hours, 12 hours, 24 hours, immediate, 30 days) and different recipients (OSHA, NRC, SERC, LEPC, EPA region).

datasets.title: Industrial VFD fault and alarm codes by brand
datasets.description: What the fault and alarm codes on the display of an industrial variable-frequency drive (VFD) stand for, taken from each manufacturer's own manual. Codes are short strings that look alike across brands and mean different things: 13 is over current on a Danfoss VLT and a ground fault on an Allen-Bradley PowerFlex 40. Each record gives the code exactly as the keypad shows it, the name the manual prints beside it, and — where the manual grades events — whether it is a warning the drive keeps running through or a fault that trips it. The corrective action is not reproduced here; the linked manual page has it.

datasets.title: How long an insurer has to acknowledge, decide and pay a claim, by state: statutory and regulatory claim-handling deadlines
datasets.description: The deadlines each US state puts on an insurance company handling a claim: how many days to acknowledge that a claim was received, how many days to reply to a policyholder's communication, how many days to accept or deny the claim after receiving proof of loss, how many days to pay once it has accepted, and what interest or penalty runs if it misses. Each record is one deadline in one state, carrying the number of days exactly as the state writes it, whether they are calendar, business or working days, the event the clock starts from, the citation to the statute or administrative rule that sets it, and the verbatim sentence. Answers 'how long does an insurance company have to pay a claim in Texas', 'what is the deadline for an insurer to deny a claim', 'how many days does my insurer have to acknowledge my claim in Ohio', and 'my insurer has had my proof of loss for 46 days — has a deadline passed'. No single original exists: every state adopted its own version of the NAIC Unfair Claims Settlement Practices model, half of them in a statute and half in an administrative rule, and NAIC's own topic page for it is now a 404.

datasets.title: State life and health insurance guaranty association benefit limits — how much is protected if your insurer fails
datasets.description: Every US state runs a life/health insurance guaranty association — a state-chartered backstop, funded by assessments on other insurers, that pays policyholders (up to a cap) if their life, annuity, disability, long-term-care or health insurer becomes insolvent. FDIC/SIPC-style protection, but almost nobody outside the insurance industry knows it exists or what it actually covers, because unlike bank deposit insurance there is no single federal number — each state sets its own dollar caps by statute, and the caps genuinely differ: California caps life death benefit at $300,000 and lumps all health benefits into one $200,000, CPI-adjusted figure; Florida caps life at just $100,000 (cash value only) but health benefit plans at $500,000; Virginia splits accident-and-sickness coverage into four separate tiers (general, disability income, long-term care, health benefit plans) with different caps for each. Answers 'is my life insurance policy protected if the company goes under', 'how much of my annuity would I actually get back', and 'why did my neighbor in another state get a different payout' — the kind of question someone asks in the middle of an actual insurer failure, when the industry's own explainer (NOLHGA) is a member-funded index, not a citable comparison table.

datasets.title: Interstate Professional Licensure Compact Participation by State
datasets.description: Which U.S. states participate in which interstate licensure compacts (nursing, psychology, physical therapy, counseling, social work, EMS, occupational therapy, audiology/speech pathology, dietetics, physician assistant, respiratory care, school psychology, athletic training), with effective dates and enabling statute citations.

datasets.title: Intrastate truck driver hours-of-service rules by state — where they differ from federal
datasets.description: The hours-of-service rules for commercial drivers operating solely within one state, per state: maximum driving hours per shift, the on-duty window, the weekly/cycle cap, the short-haul air-mile radius, and whether the state simply adopts the federal rules unchanged (which is itself an answer worth stating). Federal 49 CFR 395 does not apply intrastate; states set their own, and they genuinely differ — Florida allows 12 driving hours in a 16-hour window against the federal 11-in-14 (Fla. Stat. 316.302), California allows 12 hours and an 80-in-8 cycle (13 CCR 1212). Answers 'how many hours can I drive if I never leave Texas', 'does the 14-hour rule apply intrastate in Florida', and the questions small intrastate carriers and their drivers ask without a compliance department to ask instead. No neutral cross-state compilation exists; the search results and page-one content contradict each other about Texas.

datasets.title: Withdrawn and superseded ISO standards
datasets.description: Every deliverable in ISO's own open-data register that has been withdrawn or superseded, with the successor ISO names for it. Answers 'ISO 9001:2008 withdrawn — replaced by what', 'is ISO 13485:2003 still current', and 'what replaced IEC 31010:2009' — the lookup assistants get confidently wrong on an obscure designation, because the supersession chain is versioned, scattered across editions, and only ever published as a machine-readable file. 24,542 records read from the ISO Open Data CSV on 2026-08-05, each quoting the CSV row it came from. Rendered as pages of 100 rather than one page per standard: the source is a single machine-readable file, so a page per record would be 24,542 restatements of one download.

datasets.title: GC column stationary phase cross-reference by manufacturer
datasets.description: A cross-reference of gas chromatography (GC) capillary column stationary phases across manufacturers, showing which column product names from Agilent, Restek, Phenomenex, Supelco/Merck, GL Sciences, GS-Tek, Trajan/SGE, Macherey-Nagel, Quadrex, PerkinElmer, and others correspond to the same underlying phase chemistry. Each record is one stationary phase family (e.g. '100% dimethylpolysiloxane' or 'polyethylene glycol'), identified by its chemical composition and USP G-code(s), with the equivalent column product names from each manufacturer listed. Built from the published cross-reference tables of three column manufacturers (GL Sciences, GS-Tek, Restek), each of which maps its own products to competitors'. No single original publishes this for all manufacturers — every vendor's table is one-directional, listing only its own equivalents to competitors. The synthesis value is in merging them into a single multi-directional lookup. Answers 'what GC column from Restek is equivalent to an Agilent DB-5ms', 'what USP G-code does this phase carry', 'which manufacturers make a 14% cyanopropylphenyl column', and 'what is the phase chemistry of a ZB-WAX column'.

datasets.title: Accuracy classes and maximum permissible errors for trade measuring instruments (EU MID)
datasets.description: Accuracy classes and maximum permissible errors that Directive 2014/32/EU (the Measuring Instruments Directive) assigns to instruments used for trade in the EU. Each record is one instrument type at one accuracy class under one measurement condition, with the permitted error the directive states. Covers the ten instrument-specific annexes: water meters (MI-001), gas meters and volume conversion devices (MI-002), active electrical energy meters (MI-003), thermal energy meters (MI-004), measuring systems for liquids other than water including fuel dispensers and road tankers (MI-005), automatic weighing instruments (MI-006), taximeters (MI-007), material measures (MI-008), dimensional measuring instruments (MI-009) and exhaust gas analysers (MI-010). Answers 'what is the maximum permissible error for a water meter', 'what accuracy class does a petrol pump have to be', 'MID accuracy class for a taximeter', 'allowed error on a weighbridge', 'thermal energy meter accuracy class 2 MPE' and 'is my fuel dispenser within tolerance'. The values are condition-dependent -- the error allowed at low flow differs from the error allowed at high flow, and in-service limits differ from new-instrument limits -- so a single percentage figure is almost always the wrong answer. A deliberate mirror: there is one original, but the numbers sit in ten annexes of a 300,000-character legal text with no per-instrument row structure, and search engines currently answer this question from document-sharing sites and equipment vendors rather than from the directive.

datasets.title: What a newspaper may legally charge to publish a legal notice — by US state
datasets.description: Every self-storage lien sale, foreclosure, probate, name change, DBA filing, estate notice and municipal budget in the United States has to be published as a paid legal notice in a qualifying newspaper, and in most states the price the newspaper may charge is capped by statute. This is a state-by-state comparison of that cap, taken from the statute itself rather than from a compilation. The statutes do not share a unit: Nebraska and Colorado cap cents per line of a specified type size and column width, Ohio and West Virginia work in column inches, Wyoming and Kansas in cents per word or per line with banding, and Alabama, Arkansas, Arizona and Washington set no number at all but tie the legal rate to the newspaper's own lowest commercial or classified rate. Several states charge a lower rate for the second and subsequent insertions of the same notice. Iowa's statutory figure is a base rate that the department of administrative services recalculates every June by CPI and publishes in the Iowa Administrative Bulletin, so the statute alone does not give the current number. The point of the comparison is that it is unit-normalised, dated, and read off the current statute: the leading free compilation in this niche still quotes Nebraska's 1996 rate of forty-five cents per line, where the statute has said fifty cents per line since October 1, 2023. Answers 'how much can a newspaper charge me to run a legal notice', 'is the price I was quoted for a foreclosure or lien-sale notice legal', and 'what is the legal advertising rate in my state'. Relevant to self-storage operators, foreclosure trustees, probate lawyers, county clerks, municipal budget officers, and the newspapers selling the notices.

datasets.title: Life insurance premium grace periods and lapse protections by US state
datasets.description: For each US state, the minimum grace period its insurance code requires a life insurance policy to allow after a missed premium before the policy may lapse, plus any additional lapse protections (extended periods for seniors, designated-third-party notice requirements) — sourced from each state's insurance code. Answers 'how long is the life insurance grace period in [state]', 'can my life insurance lapse after one missed payment', and 'does the insurer have to notify anyone before my policy lapses'. Most states require 30 or 31 days, but California requires not less than 60 days plus a 30-day pre-lapse notice to the owner and any designated third party (Ins. Code § 10113.71) — generic web content still says '30 or 31 days' everywhere, so the unaided answer is wrong exactly where a statute moved.

datasets.title: LIHEAP income eligibility limits by state and household size
datasets.description: LIHEAP (federal home heating/cooling energy assistance) sets a national floor -- 110% of the federal poverty guideline, or 60% of state median income if higher -- but leaves the actual cutoff to each state, and states pick anywhere up to 150-175% FPG or their own SMI schedule and re-publish it once a year in dollars per household size. The one federal aggregator (the LIHEAP Clearinghouse) that used to compile all 50 states into one table is unreachable (SSL certificate failure, verified 2026-08-20) and third-party benefit-screening sites reproduce it without sourcing which state page they read it from or when. Each record is one state x one household size x one program season, stating the income ceiling, whether it is annual or monthly, and the percent-of-FPG or SMI basis the state used. Answers 'do I qualify for LIHEAP in [state] with a household of [n] and [income]', 'what's the LIHEAP income limit for a family of 4 in [state] this year'.

datasets.title: Lithium battery shipping limits (49 CFR 173.185)
datasets.description: Watt-hour and lithium-content thresholds, quantity limits and packaging conditions for shipping lithium cells and batteries under US hazardous materials regulations. Deliberately NOT a compatibility table — this is regulatory prose with numeric triggers, and it tests whether the pipeline handles a non-tabular asset.

datasets.title: ACA marketplace subsidy income limits by coverage year, household size and state group
datasets.description: The dollar income limits that decide whether a household qualifies for an ACA premium tax credit, for each coverage year, each household size from 1 to 8, and each of the three federal poverty guideline schedules (48 contiguous states and DC, Alaska, Hawaii). Each record states the poverty guideline the marketplace actually applies to that coverage year, the dollar figures at the 100%, 138%, 150%, 200%, 250%, 300% and 400% marks, the share of income the household is expected to pay at the top of the scale, and whether a hard cutoff applies above 400%. The enhanced credits created by the American Rescue Plan Act and extended by the Inflation Reduction Act lapsed on 31 December 2025, so coverage year 2026 was the first year since 2020 in which a household above 400% of the poverty line received no credit at all. No single page states these dollar figures. HHS publishes the poverty guidelines without the ACA multiples; the IRS publishes the applicable percentages without any dollar amounts; and the marketplace applies the guidelines published before open enrollment opened, not the guidelines bearing the coverage year's own number, which is the step most secondary sources get wrong. Answers 'what is the income limit for marketplace insurance in [year]', 'what is 400% of the federal poverty level for a family of [n]', 'how much can I earn and still get an Obamacare subsidy', 'what is the subsidy cliff', and 'what percentage of income do I have to pay for a benchmark plan'.

datasets.title: Mechanics lien filing deadlines, preliminary notice requirements, and enforcement windows by US state and party role
datasets.description: State-by-state comparison of the deadlines that determine whether a contractor, subcontractor, or material supplier keeps or loses the right to file a mechanics lien on a construction project. Each record is one state with the preliminary notice deadline (days from first furnishing), lien recording deadline (days from completion or last furnishing), and enforcement deadline (days from recording to file suit), broken out by party role (general contractor vs subcontractor/supplier). Also captures whether preliminary notice is required at all, the notice name in each state's statute, whether the state is a 'full price lien' or 'unpaid balance' state, and the statutory citation. Answers 'how many days do I have to file a lien in [state] as a [sub/supplier]', 'do I need to send preliminary notice in [state]', and 'what happens if I miss the deadline'.

datasets.title: How long medical certificates last for pilots, commercial drivers and merchant mariners — by class, age and service type
datasets.description: How long a federally required medical certificate remains valid for each regulated transport occupation, and what it depends on. FAA pilot medicals (14 CFR 61.23) cascade by class and age — a first-class certificate carries first-class privileges to the 12th month for pilots under 40 but only the 6th month at 40 or older, then downgrades to second- and third-class privileges on a schedule; commercial drivers need a medical examiner's certificate on a cycle set by 49 CFR 391.45; merchant mariner medical certificates run 2 years for STCW service but 5 years for national-only credentials, and only 1 year for mariners under 18 (46 CFR 10.301). Same question — 'how long is my medical good for?' — three regulators, three completely different answer structures. Answers 'how long is a first class medical valid for a 45-year-old pilot?', 'how often does a truck driver need a DOT physical?', 'why is my mariner medical certificate only valid two years?'

datasets.title: US minimum wage rates by state, city, and worker type
datasets.description: Current minimum wage, tipped (subminimum) wage, and small-employer rates for every US state plus major cities and counties that set their own higher rate. Each record is one jurisdiction at one worker type, stating the current hourly rate, effective date, next scheduled change, and the indexing method if any. Answers 'what is the minimum wage in [city/state]', 'what is the tipped wage in [state]', and 'when does the minimum wage go up in [jurisdiction]'.

datasets.title: How far off a US fuel pump, LPG meter or EV charger is allowed to be (NIST Handbook 44)
datasets.description: The accuracy every commercial device that sells fuel or energy in the United States has to hold, taken from NIST Handbook 44 -- the specifications and tolerances that state weights-and-measures programs adopt by reference and enforce when they inspect a gas pump. Each record is one row of one tolerance table: the commodity or device the row covers, its accuracy class, and the three limits the handbook prints for it. Answers 'how accurate does a gas pump have to be' (a retail petrol or diesel dispenser is Accuracy Class 0.5: 0.5 % once in service, 0.3 % when newly installed), 'is a new dispenser held to a tighter standard than one already in service' (yes -- the acceptance tolerance for a new or newly repaired device is tighter than the maintenance tolerance that applies afterwards), and the same question for propane, anhydrous ammonia, CNG, hydrogen, liquid CO2, cryogenic products and EV chargers. Covers Handbook 44 sections 3.30 (liquid-measuring devices), 3.31 (vehicle-tank meters), 3.32 (LPG and anhydrous ammonia), 3.33 (hydrocarbon gas vapor), 3.34 (cryogenic), 3.37 (mass flow meters), 3.38 (carbon dioxide), 3.39 (hydrogen) and 3.40 (electric vehicle fueling systems). Three things to read alongside the numbers. First, the handbook footnotes that special test tolerances do not apply to retail motor fuel or retail Diesel Exhaust Fluid dispensers at all, so the special-test column in section 3.30 is not a limit a filling-station pump is held to; that footnote is carried here as its own record. Second, the Accuracy Class 0.5 percentages stop applying on a small test draft: in section 3.30, a draft of 40 L (10 gal) or less is held to a volume figure instead of a percentage, and in section 3.31 to 6 in3 for a 5 gallon draft and 11 in3 for a 10 gallon one. The section 3.30 version of that exception is a record here. Third, this is a first pass over a source published only as a PDF: a table row is included only where the device, the class and the printed limits sit in one continuous run of text, so a handful of rows whose bullets are split across a page break by the PDF's running footer are not yet here -- section 3.30's Accuracy Class 0.3 row is the notable omission, and the equivalent row is present from sections 3.31 and 3.37. Nothing is reconstructed across a break; a row we cannot quote whole is left out.

datasets.title: State below-cost motor fuel selling laws and minimum-markup percentages
datasets.description: A handful of states make it illegal for a gas station to sell fuel below its own cost, on the theory that a chain with deep pockets could otherwise sell at a loss long enough to drive independent competitors out and then raise prices. Two separate things have to be known before anyone can act on one of these laws, and they almost always live in two different statute sections: what conduct is actually prohibited (and what the exceptions are), and how the law says 'cost' is calculated. So each state gets a record for each. Only two of the states here bolt a fixed cost-of-doing-business markup percentage onto cost -- Wisconsin (6% retail, 3% wholesale, 9.18% on the average posted terminal price) and West Virginia (4% wholesale) -- which is why the popular name 'minimum markup law' is misleading everywhere else: Minnesota, Missouri, North Carolina and Florida set a cost floor with no fixed percentage on top. No comprehensive compiled version of these laws was found; each state's rule lives only in its own statute or agency guidance page. Answers 'can a gas station legally sell below cost in my state', 'what's the minimum markup percentage for gasoline in Wisconsin', 'what counts as cost for a gas station in Florida', 'is meeting a competitor's price an exception'.

datasets.title: National Electrical Code edition adopted by each US state
datasets.description: For each US state: which edition of the National Electrical Code (NEC) is currently in force statewide, the name of the state code that adopts it (e.g. the 2023 Oregon Electrical Specialty Code), its effective date, whether the state amends the NEC, and whether adoption of a newer edition is underway. Answers 'which NEC edition applies in [state]', 'has [state] adopted the 2026 NEC', and 'when did the [year] NEC take effect in [state]'. This is the supersession/adoption-chain shape the portfolio has not tried. The retrieval slot is unusually open: NFPA's own enforcement map — the authoritative assembly — returns a 39-character JS shell to a plain HTTP client, so no agent can read it; page one is electrician-prep and label-vendor blogs that disagree with each other (one lists 7 states on NEC 2026 as of July 2026, another says zero as of March 2026, and one lists Oregon as adopted-2026 while Oregon's own building-codes page shows the 2023 OESC current with 2026 adoption only underway). The authority per state is the state's electrical board, building-codes agency, or administrative code — the same statute/board hosts as the built electrician-licence-progression asset, this portfolio's best-scoring publisher type. Caveat to state on the page: local jurisdictions (AHJs) may enforce a different edition; this asset records statewide adoption only.

datasets.title: Which National Electrical Code edition each US state enforces: adoption status, effective dates and amendments, from the state boards themselves
datasets.description: The NEC edition currently in force in each US state, with the effective date, the adopting authority, whether state amendments apply, and any announced transition to a newer edition. The spread is real and moving: Minnesota has adopted the 2026 NEC effective Aug. 17, 2026 (permits filed before that date follow the 2023 NEC); Oregon's 2023 Oregon Electrical Specialty Code, based on the 2023 NEC, took effect Oct. 1, 2023 with a published table of amendments; other states remain on the 2020 or 2017 editions, and several have no statewide adoption at all, leaving it to local jurisdictions. Answers 'which NEC edition is in effect in my state?', 'which states have adopted the 2026 NEC?', 'does my state amend the NEC or adopt it unamended?', 'when does the new electrical code take effect for permits?'

datasets.title: EPA NESHAP Source Category Applicability Crosswalk
datasets.description: Maps each EPA NESHAP source category to its 40 CFR subpart, whether it applies to major or area sources, the original final rule date, most recent amendment, and residual risk/technology review status.

datasets.title: NFA firearm category definitions and current transfer/making tax
datasets.description: The National Firearms Act regulates six firearm categories -- short-barreled rifle, short-barreled shotgun, any other weapon (AOW), machine gun, silencer, destructive device -- each defined by its own measurement threshold in ATF's regulations at 27 CFR 478.11 and 479.11. Separately, and recently changed: the federal transfer tax and making tax on those items dropped from $200 per item to $0 for every category except machine guns and destructive devices, under section 70436 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (Pub. L. 119-21, signed 2025-07-04), which amended 26 U.S.C. 5811(a) and 5821(a). ATF states the change took effect on January 1, 2026, and issued a final rule on 2026-05-08 (ATF No. 2025R-45F, 91 FR 25112) conforming 27 CFR 479.61, 479.62, 479.81, 479.82 and 479.84 to the new rates. Each record is one NFA category, giving its defining measurement threshold and its current and prior transfer/making tax, each quoted verbatim from the regulation or from ATF's own rulemaking. Two things vendor pages routinely get wrong: the paperwork did not change (Form 1/Form 4, fingerprints and the background check are all unchanged), and the AOW transfer tax went from $5 -- not $200 -- to $0. One nuance not carried per-record: the short-barreled rifle and shotgun definitions here are 27 CFR 478.11's, which are the ones that name those terms; the NFA's own list at 27 CFR 479.11(b) and (d) states the 'weapon made from a rifle/shotgun' prong slightly more broadly, as an overall length under 26 inches OR a barrel under 16 (rifle) / 18 (shotgun) inches. Answers 'what barrel length makes a rifle an SBR', 'how much is an ATF tax stamp in 2026', 'is the NFA tax still $200'.

datasets.title: NFPA 704 fire diamond ratings by chemical
datasets.description: The NFPA 704 'fire diamond' rating for a chemical — the health (blue), flammability (red), instability (yellow) numbers and any special (white) notice — as published on that chemical's own datasheet. Each record is one chemical, with the four quadrants and the datasheet's own wording for what each value means. Answers 'what is the NFPA 704 rating for anhydrous ammonia', 'fire diamond numbers for thionyl chloride', and 'what does a 3 in the blue diamond mean'. NFPA 704 itself is a paywalled standard and the per-chemical ratings are scattered one page at a time across datasheets and SDSs, so no single free table exists — assembly, one source per record.

datasets.title: NIST cryptographic algorithm deprecation schedule: what is approved, deprecated, and disallowed, and when
datasets.description: Per-algorithm status under NIST guidance for the post-quantum cryptographic transition. Each record is one algorithm or key-length configuration with its current approval status (approved, acceptable, deprecated, restricted, disallowed, legacy use), the date at which the status changes, and the recommended replacement. Drawn from three NIST publications: IR 8547 (post-quantum transition timeline), SP 800-131A Rev 2 (current algorithm status rules) and Rev 3 draft (upcoming changes), and FIPS 203/204/205 (the post-quantum replacement standards). The key deadlines: quantum-vulnerable public-key algorithms (RSA, ECDSA, ECDH, finite-field DH) deprecated after 2030, disallowed after 2035; SHA-1 and 224-bit hashes deprecated through 2030, disallowed thereafter. AES-256 and SHA-2/SHA-3 are NOT on the deprecation schedule. Answers 'when is RSA deprecated?', 'is AES-256 affected by the post-quantum transition?', 'what replaces ECDSA?', and 'what is the current NIST status of 3DES?'

datasets.title: Current EPA nonattainment county designations by pollutant
datasets.description: Whether a US county is in 'nonattainment' for a given Clean Air Act pollutant (and if so, at what severity classification) drives real obligations for anyone building, permitting, or selling into that county: stricter new-source review, vehicle inspection and reformulated-fuel requirements, and federal highway-funding conditions all key off this status. EPA's Green Book is the single authoritative list, but it is a very long plain-text table with no per-county lookup and no API — a resident, contractor, or small manufacturer has to scan hundreds of rows by hand to find their county. Each record is one county x one pollutant NAAQS combination: whether it is designated nonattainment, the classification if the pollutant test has one (Marginal through Extreme for ozone; Moderate/Serious for PM), and the named nonattainment area it belongs to. Answers 'is [county] in nonattainment for ozone', 'what classification is [county] for PM-2.5', 'does building in [county] trigger nonattainment-area permitting'.

datasets.title: US state notifiable disease reporting timeframes by condition
datasets.description: State-by-state reporting timeframes for notifiable diseases and conditions. Each record is one state’s reporting requirement for one disease, with the mandated timeframe (immediately, 4 hours, 24 hours, 3 working days, 7 days, etc.), the reporting method (telephone, fax, electronic), and the receiving agency. Answers 'how quickly must I report [disease] in [state]', 'which diseases require immediate telephone reporting in [state]', 'what is the reporting timeframe for measles in Georgia vs Kansas'. The matrix is roughly 50 states × 80+ conditions, and no cross-state comparison exists despite every state publishing its own list individually.

datasets.title: Deprecated npm packages and their maintainer-named replacement
datasets.description: npm allows a maintainer to attach a 'deprecated' message to a specific published version, and that message often names the exact replacement package or built-in API to use instead -- 'left-pad' points at String.prototype.padStart(), 'istanbul' points at nyc, 'tslint' points at ESLint, 'babel-eslint' points at @babel/eslint-parser. This is first-party, machine-readable data sitting in the registry API itself, but nobody has assembled it into a browsable table: a developer running `npm install` sees the warning once in a terminal scroll and it is gone, and the alternative is a content-mill blog post ranking '10 request alternatives' without quoting what the maintainer actually said. This asset would have been too tedious to maintain by hand across thousands of packages -- watching a firehose of new deprecations and re-checking old ones for changes -- but is a mechanical registry read for one machine, refreshable on a schedule at zero marginal cost per package. Each record is one deprecated package, quoting its maintainer's own deprecated message verbatim and naming the specific replacement stated in it. Answers 'is request deprecated', 'what should I use instead of tslint', 'why is my npm install warning about gulp-util'.

datasets.title: Which OSHA NRTL is recognized for which test standard: all 21 labs' scopes of recognition, cross-referenced
datasets.description: For every OSHA Nationally Recognized Testing Laboratory (NRTL), each test standard the lab is currently recognized for, taken from the lab's own scope-of-recognition page on osha.gov. One record per lab-standard pair. OSHA publishes each lab's scope on a separate page and publishes no cross-lab view, so answering 'which NRTLs can certify to UL 507?' or 'is DEKRA recognized for ANSI/AAMI ES 60601-1?' or 'which labs besides UL can certify commercial cooking appliances?' today means opening up to 21 pages and searching each one. The recognition matters commercially: a product that 29 CFR 1910.7 requires to be NRTL-certified must be certified by a lab whose scope covers the applicable standard, and manufacturers choosing a lab, buyers verifying a certification mark, and safety engineers checking whether a mark is valid for a given standard all need the standard-to-lab direction that OSHA does not publish.

datasets.title: Which OSHA-recognized labs (NRTLs) can certify to a given test standard
datasets.description: The inverted view of OSHA's Nationally Recognized Testing Laboratory program: for each test standard, every NRTL currently recognized to certify products to it. Answers 'which NRTLs can certify to UL 508A', 'can anyone other than UL list to UL 1741', 'is my lab's mark acceptable to OSHA for this product', and 'who else could quote this job'. OSHA publishes the recognition one laboratory at a time — twenty separate pages, each a long table of that lab's standards — and its own list-of-standards page says so in as many words: 'See individual NRTL informational web pages to determine which of these standards fall within an NRTL's scope of recognition.' So the question a manufacturer actually has (who may certify my product, and therefore who can I ask for a price) requires opening and searching twenty pages, and nobody publishes the answer.

datasets.title: Nursing home minimum staffing requirements by US state — hours per resident day and RN coverage mandates after the 2026 federal repeal
datasets.description: State-by-state comparison of legally mandated minimum staffing levels for nursing homes (skilled nursing facilities). Each record is one state with the total hours of nursing care per resident per day (HPRD), the RN-specific HPRD minimum, the CNA-specific HPRD minimum, the RN coverage requirement (hours per day), and the statutory citation. The federal CMS minimum (3.48 HPRD + 24/7 RN) was REPEALED in December 2025, effective February 2026, and a moratorium through October 2034 was enacted via the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. States are now the only authority. State values are drawn from the Consumer Voice 50-state staffing standards chart (November 2021), except New York and South Carolina, which come from the state agencies directly; state law changes since November 2021 may not be reflected. Answers 'what is the minimum nursing staff my state requires per resident' and 'is there still a federal nursing home staffing minimum'.

datasets.title: Nursing homes under CMS Special Focus Facility oversight: current SFFs, candidates, graduates and terminations, by CMS certification number
datasets.description: Which US nursing homes are in the CMS Special Focus Facility (SFF) programme, which are candidates for it, which have graduated and which have left Medicare and Medicaid altogether. Each record is one facility, identified by its six-digit CMS certification number (provider number), carrying the facility name, address, city, state, ZIP and phone exactly as CMS prints them, which of the four tables it appears in, the date of its most recent inspection, whether that inspection met the graduation criteria, and how many months it has been an SFF. Answers 'is this nursing home a special focus facility', 'which nursing homes in Ohio are on the SFF list', 'how long has this home been under enhanced oversight', 'which homes graduated from the SFF program', and 'which nursing homes were terminated from Medicare'. CMS publishes this as a single PDF that is overwritten every month, with no archive index, no per-facility page and no statement of what changed, so a month-stamped question — and people search month-stamped, see the autocomplete evidence in state/territories/nursing-home-special-focus-facilities.json — has no published answer at all.

datasets.title: OSHA fall protection trigger height by standard
datasets.description: OSHA does not set one fall-protection trigger height. General industry (29 CFR 1910.28) sets 4 feet, general construction (1926.501) sets 6 feet, scaffolds (1926.451) sets 10 feet, and steel erection (1926.760) sets 15 feet -- the same worker doing the same job can cross from one trigger to another by changing which standard applies. Nor does any one standard set a single height: within general industry a fixed ladder triggers at 24 feet, a repair pit is exempt below 10 feet, and low-slope roof work is governed by distance from the edge rather than height at all. Each record is one named hazard situation inside one standard -- the numbered paragraph the regulation itself uses, such as 'Hoist areas', 'Holes' or 'Steep roofs' -- stating the height that triggers protection there and exactly what the paragraph requires once it does, quoted from the regulation. Safety consultants and OSHA-training blogs restate the 4/6/10/15 numbers constantly but rarely cite the paragraph or state what is required, which is the part that matters for compliance. Answers 'what height do I need fall protection at', 'is scaffold fall protection 6 feet or 10 feet', 'what height do I need fall protection around a floor hole', 'what OSHA standard covers steel erection fall protection'.

datasets.title: OSHA medical surveillance trigger thresholds by substance
datasets.description: The airborne exposure level that triggers mandatory medical surveillance under each OSHA substance-specific standard (29 CFR 1910 Subpart Z), compared across all regulated substances. Each record is one substance, carrying its action level, PEL, the exposure duration that triggers surveillance, the medical exam scope and frequency, biological monitoring requirements if any, and the record retention period. Answers 'what is the action level for lead', 'at what exposure must I provide medical exams for benzene workers', 'how often does cadmium biological monitoring need to happen', and 'which OSHA substances require 40-year record retention'. The action level is typically half the PEL but not always, and the surveillance trigger conditions vary wildly: lead uses blood lead levels, cadmium uses urine cadmium, and most others use airborne concentration plus days-per-year thresholds.

datasets.title: OSHA injury and illness recordkeeping exemptions by industry (NAICS)
datasets.description: Whether a business must keep OSHA 300 injury/illness logs turns on two independent rules that no single page states together: a company-size exemption (10 or fewer employees, company-wide, at any time in the last calendar year) under 29 CFR 1904.1, and a partial industry exemption for specific NAICS codes under 29 CFR 1904 Subpart B Appendix A, which applies regardless of size. Each record is one partially-exempt industry, carrying its NAICS code and the regulation's own industry label. Separate page-level notes carry what the exemption actually does (and the written-request condition that suspends it), that the industry exemption attaches to an establishment rather than a whole company, the company-size rule, and the fatality/hospitalization/amputation/eye-loss reporting requirement that survives both exemptions. Answers 'does a gas station have to keep an OSHA log', 'is my software company exempt from OSHA recordkeeping', 'do I still have to report a fatality if I'm exempt', 'my company has an exempt office and a non-exempt warehouse'.

datasets.title: OSHA training requirements by standard: topic, frequency, and CFR citation
datasets.description: Which OSHA standards require employee training, what the training must cover, how often it must be repeated, and who must receive it. Each record is one training requirement tied to a specific CFR section. Training frequencies vary: some are annual (respiratory protection 1910.134, bloodborne pathogens 1910.1030), some are event-driven (lockout/tagout 1910.147 — retrain when procedures change), some are initial-only with situational retraining (PPE 1910.132). Answers 'what OSHA training does my construction crew need', 'how often is respiratory protection training required', and 'does OSHA require annual forklift certification'.

datasets.title: Outboard motor service specifications by brand and model
datasets.description: Spark plug, gap, oil capacity, oil filter, gear lube capacity and water pump impeller kit part numbers for outboard motors by brand and model range. One row per model or model range. Answers 'what spark plug does my Yamaha F150 take?', 'Yamaha F150 water pump repair kit part number', and 'Mercury serial number year chart' — questions where assistants guess a plausible but wrong part number, capacity or model year.

datasets.title: Packaging specification equivalence: neck finishes, corrugated grades and pallet standards
datasets.description: Cross-reference of packaging specifications that procurement, packaging engineers and brand owners need when substituting materials, matching closures to bottles, or converting between regional standards. Covers three domains: (1) SPI/GPI plastic and glass neck-finish dimensions with tolerances (T, E, H, S, I) for the 400, 410 and 415 thread series; (2) corrugated board grade equivalence between Mullen burst test and ECT edge crush test ratings, with maximum weight limits from both the Fibre Box Handbook and UPS guidelines; (3) EUR/ISO pallet footprint dimensions, load ratings and regional designations. Answers questions like 'what are the T and E dimensions for a 24-410 finish', 'is 200# Mullen the same as 32 ECT', and 'what size is a EUR 2 pallet'.

datasets.title: PDMP Mandatory Prescriber Check Requirements by State
datasets.description: When and for which drugs each US state requires prescribers to check the Prescription Drug Monitoring Program before prescribing controlled substances, with trigger conditions, exemptions, re-check intervals, and statutory citations.

datasets.title: US EPA pesticide residue tolerance limits by active ingredient and crop commodity
datasets.description: What is the maximum legal pesticide residue allowed on this food in the United States? EPA sets tolerances in 40 CFR Part 180, one section per active ingredient, each listing ppm limits by crop or crop group. There are ~500 sections and no single cross-reference table exists. This asset assembles them: one record per active ingredient × commodity, with the ppm tolerance, the CFR section, and the crop group. Answers 'glyphosate tolerance on soybeans', 'what is the MRL for chlorpyrifos on apples', 'EPA pesticide tolerance list by crop'. Food importers check tolerances against shipment lab results; farmers compare tolerances when choosing pesticide products.

datasets.title: PFAS drinking water concentration limits by US state — MCLs, notification levels, action levels, and health advisories for PFOA, PFOS, and other per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances
datasets.description: State-by-state comparison of legally enforceable and advisory concentration limits for PFAS compounds in drinking water. Each record is one state–chemical pair with the concentration limit (in parts per trillion), the regulation type (MCL, notification level, action level, health advisory, or guideline), the effective date, the statutory or regulatory citation, and whether the state limit is stricter than the federal EPA MCL. The federal MCLs are 4 ppt for PFOA and PFOS (affirmed May 2025); MCLs for PFHxS, PFNA, and HFPO-DA are under proposed rescission as of May 2026. State limits range from 0.00266 ppt (Nevada, PFOA) to 400,000 ppt (Michigan, PFHxA). Answers 'what is the legal PFAS limit in my state', 'is my state stricter than the federal standard', and 'which PFAS compounds does my state regulate'.

datasets.title: State pharmacy technician-to-pharmacist supervision ratios
datasets.description: The maximum number of pharmacy technicians a single pharmacist may supervise in each US state, with the practice setting it applies to and any conditions that raise or lower the cap. Each record is one jurisdiction with its ratio rule, the practice setting (community/retail, hospital/institutional, or both), whether conditional increases apply (e.g., higher ratio if technicians are certified, if automated dispensing is in use, or if the setting is institutional), and the regulatory citation. Answers 'how many techs can I supervise in Ohio' (no cap on licensed technicians; max 3 trainees), 'does California allow a higher ratio for certified techs', 'which states have no fixed ratio', and 'what is the pharmacist-to-tech ratio in a hospital in Connecticut'. States range from strict 1:2 caps (Connecticut community, New York community, Tennessee) to no fixed cap (Arizona, Colorado, Florida, Idaho, Iowa, Michigan, Missouri, North Carolina, Ohio, Oregon, Texas, Washington, Wisconsin — at least 13 states where professional judgment applies).

datasets.title: Pilot licence minimum hours, age and prerequisites by civil aviation authority
datasets.description: The minimum flight hours, minimum age, solo and cross-country requirements and prerequisite licences for each pilot licence and rating, compared across the FAA (United States), EASA (European Union), the UK CAA (retained Part-FCL) and Transport Canada. One record is one stated requirement for one licence under one authority, with the provision citation. Answers 'how many hours do I need for a private pilot licence UK vs US', 'FAA PPL minimum flight hours 61.109', 'EASA PPL 45 hours', 'minimum age for a commercial pilot licence Canada', 'can simulator time count towards a PPL', and 'how many hours to convert an FAA PPL to a UK licence'. The UK kept the EU article numbering after Brexit and then changed the number inside it: FCL.210.A(a) reads 45 hours in EU law and 40 hours in UK retained law, amended with effect from 1 October 2025 by S.I. 2025/878. Same provision identifier, two different values, one of them recent.

datasets.title: Plumbing fitting and pipe thread standards
datasets.description: Dimensional specifications for NPT and BSP pipe thread sizes used in plumbing, hydraulic, and gas fittings worldwide. For each nominal pipe size within each standard, gives threads per inch, pitch, major diameter, and minor diameter — the numbers needed to identify an unknown thread or confirm whether two fittings will mate. Combines American (ASME B1.20.1) and British/ISO (ISO 228, ISO 7) standards in one table so the critical differences are visible side by side.

datasets.title: Planned US generating-unit retirements, as EIA published them in one named month's Electric Power Monthly
datasets.description: Every utility-scale US electric generating unit its operator has told EIA it plans to retire, as printed in a single named monthly edition of EIA's Electric Power Monthly: the planned retirement month and year, the plant and unit it belongs to, the operating company, the state, the net summer capacity in megawatts, the generating technology, the fuel and the prime mover. Each record is one generating unit as one edition reported it, and every page names the edition it was read from. Answers 'when is the J.H. Campbell plant retiring', 'which generating units in Illinois are scheduled to retire in 2027' and 'how much coal capacity is scheduled to come off the grid next year' — for the edition named on the page. It does not answer whether a unit's date has moved since an earlier filing: we hold one edition, EIA overwrites the previous month's figure when it publishes the next one, and the back issues are PDF and ZIP only, so nothing earlier can be recovered. These plans do move — EIA's own coverage notes that 'these plans may be more subject to change than usual, with policy shifts recently delaying retirements at several coal plants' — so the edition stamp is part of the fact, not a footnote.

datasets.title: Power tool battery and accessory compatibility
datasets.description: Which power tool batteries, chargers, adapters and accessory interfaces work with which tools and platforms, from the manufacturers' and battery alliances' own pages: which brands belong to the AMPShare and CAS cross-brand 18V battery systems, which DEWALT tools the DCA1820 18V adapter fits, what FLEXVOLT batteries run in, what a Starlock or SDS shank fits, and what restrictions the manufacturer attaches. Answers 'will battery X run tool Y' and 'which brands share this battery' from the body that publishes the fact.

datasets.title: Power tool battery platform and accessory interface compatibility
datasets.description: Which power tool batteries, chargers, adapters and accessory interfaces work with which tools and brands, drawn from the manufacturers' own pages: Milwaukee M18, DEWALT 20V MAX/FLEXVOLT and the DCA1820 18V adapter fit table, RYOBI 18V ONE+, Makita LXT/XGT and the ADP10 charger adapter, the Bosch-led AMPShare alliance, the Metabo-led Cordless Alliance System (CAS), the Bosch/Fein Starlock oscillating multi-tool interface, and Heller's drill-bit shank interface guide. Answers 'does a FLEXVOLT battery work in a 20V MAX tool', 'which brands share the AMPShare / CAS 18V battery', 'will the DCA1820 adapter fit tool model X', and 'is a Starlock blade backward compatible with OIS tools' — questions where the wrong answer means a tool that will not run or a battery that will not charge.

datasets.title: What must pass before the next step: mandated step order in regulated processes
datasets.description: The mandated order of steps in multi-step regulated processes, from the authority that enforces the order: which inspection or filing must be approved before the next one may happen, what may not proceed until it passes, and the deadline attached to it. One record is one step in one authority's published sequence. Covers municipal building inspection sequences (the rough-in must pass before the wall closes; no concrete before the footing inspection) and the US import Importer Security Filing chain (ISF no later than 24 hours before lading; flexible filings finalised no later than 24 hours before arrival; cargo release withheld without an ISF). Answers 'did I need an inspection before drywall', 'what order do building inspections happen in', 'when does the ISF have to be filed', and 'what happens if the ISF is late'. The sequence is usually published only as prose on the enforcing authority's own page, one jurisdiction at a time; no comparison table exists anywhere.

datasets.title: Galvanic series and surface energy of engineering materials
datasets.description: Electrode potential in seawater (volts vs SCE) for metals and alloys from the ASM/MIL-STD-889 galvanic series, and surface energy (dyne/cm) for plastics and packaging materials. Answers 'will these two materials corrode each other' and 'will this adhesive wet this plastic'.

datasets.title: CPA continuing professional education (CPE) requirements by US jurisdiction
datasets.description: The CPE hours a licensed CPA must complete in each US state and territory to renew, as published by NASBA's National Registry of CPE Sponsors. Covers total hours, reporting period, ethics requirement, and other subject-area mandates. Answers 'how many CPE hours does a CPA need in [state]', 'what is the ethics CPE requirement for CPAs in Texas', 'which states require CPA CPE in government auditing or accounting and auditing', and 'do my CPE hours from another state count'. The scenario as briefed ('professional licensing CE by jurisdiction') spans dozens of independent regulatory datasets across professions; this asset covers CPAs because NASBA publishes a structured, per-jurisdiction page for all 55 boards of accountancy — the only profession in the scenario with a single cross-jurisdiction authority table. Nursing and insurance producer CE are different datasets with different regulators and no equivalent assembled source.

datasets.title: Property tax assessment appeal deadlines by state
datasets.description: Missing a property-tax appeal window usually forfeits the appeal for that year, and the deadline is a different shape in each state, which is what a generic answer gets wrong. Three shapes appear here: a fixed calendar date that does not move (Nevada's January 15, Nebraska's June 30, New Hampshire's March 1); a count of days running from the day a specific notice was mailed, so the date differs per property (Georgia's 45 days from the assessment notice, Kansas's 30 days from the valuation notice, Maine's 185 days from commitment); and a filing window tied to when the review body sits (Iowa's April 2 to April 30, New York's fourth Tuesday of May in most towns). Texas combines two of them — May 15 or 30 days after the notice of appraised value, whichever is later. 13 states, each with the rule quoted verbatim from the statute or agency form it comes from, and a link to that page. Answers 'when do I have to file a property tax appeal in [state]', 'how many days after my assessment notice can I protest in [state]'.

datasets.title: Pseudoephedrine purchase limits: federal gram limits and stricter state rules
datasets.description: How much pseudoephedrine (Sudafed and equivalents) a person may buy, per day and per 30 days, quoted from the statute that sets each limit. Answers 'how much Sudafed can I buy in a month', 'is pseudoephedrine prescription-only in [state]', 'why was my Sudafed purchase blocked'. Federal law caps a buyer at 9 grams in any 30 days, of which no more than 7.5 grams may arrive by post or carrier (21 U.S.C. 844(a)), and caps a seller at 3.6 grams in a calendar day (21 CFR 1314.20). Several states are stricter: Tennessee 5.76 g/30 days and 28.8 g/year, Alabama and Illinois 7.5 g/30 days, Indiana, Kentucky, Mississippi and West Virginia 7.2 g/30 days, with annual caps in Indiana (61.2 g) and West Virginia (48 g). Others are stricter in kind rather than in grams — Arkansas, Mississippi, Oregon and Tennessee allow the sale only in a pharmacy. Oregon and Mississippi are the two states the open web still gets wrong: both are routinely described as prescription-only, and the statutes quoted here say in terms that the sale is lawful without a prescription. Coverage is the federal baseline plus the 11 states listed above; a state that is absent has not been checked, not been found to match the federal floor.

datasets.title: OSHA PSM vs EPA RMP: chemical threshold quantities side by side
datasets.description: Side-by-side comparison of threshold quantities for hazardous chemicals regulated under OSHA's Process Safety Management standard (29 CFR 1910.119 Appendix A) and EPA's Risk Management Program (40 CFR 68.130). Each record is one chemical with the threshold quantity in pounds that triggers obligations under each program. Many chemicals appear on both lists with different thresholds — chlorine is 1,500 lbs under PSM and 2,500 lbs under RMP; ethylene oxide is 5,000 lbs under PSM and 10,000 lbs under RMP. EPA has ~27 chemicals not on the OSHA list and OSHA has ~79 not on EPA's. Answers 'is [chemical] covered by PSM, RMP, or both?', 'what is the threshold quantity for chlorine under each program?', and 'which chemicals have different thresholds under PSM and RMP?'

datasets.title: Reckless / excessive-speeding mph thresholds that trigger a criminal charge, by state
datasets.description: For each US state: the speed -- stated as an absolute mph, as mph over the posted limit, or both -- at which ordinary speeding stops being ordinary and the statute attaches a separate, heavier offence, quoted exactly as the statute states it, with the classification the statute gives. Answers 'how many over is reckless driving in [state]', 'what speed is reckless driving in [state]', and 'is speeding a crime in [state] or just a ticket'. The mechanism varies sharply. Virginia sets both a relative trigger (20 mph over) and an absolute one (85 mph regardless of the limit), either one alone being reckless driving. North Carolina sets the same pair as alternatives -- more than 15 over OR over 80, a Class 3 misdemeanor. Illinois sets no absolute at all, only a tiered relative one (26-34 over a Class B misdemeanor, 35+ over a Class A). Hawaii, Maine, Nevada, Colorado and Vermont each set a single threshold and each name a different kind of offence for it. And in three states the answer is that there is no criminal threshold: Arizona's excessive-speed statute has no absolute-mph clause at all (contradicting the widely repeated claim that Arizona has an '85 mph absolute' rule), Oregon keeps even 100 mph a traffic violation rather than a crime, and Ohio makes ordinary speeding a minor misdemeanor with a fourth-degree upgrade tied to district speeds rather than to mph over the limit.

datasets.title: How long federal regulations require records to be kept: retention periods, what starts the clock, and who they bind
datasets.description: The retention period each federal regulation attaches to a record type, with the trigger that starts the clock — which is where the confusion lives. OSHA employee exposure records: at least 30 years (29 CFR 1910.1020); OSHA medical records: duration of employment plus 30 years, from the same section; the OSHA 300 injury log: 5 years following the end of the covered calendar year (29 CFR 1904.33); FLSA payroll records: 3 years, but the records wage computations are based on: 2 years (29 CFR 516); HIPAA compliance documentation: 6 years from creation or last effective date, whichever is later (45 CFR 164.316); FMLA records: no less than 3 years (29 CFR 825.500); EEOC personnel records: 1 year, extended if a charge is filed (29 CFR 1602.14); driver qualification files: employment plus 3 years (49 CFR 391.51); hazardous waste manifests: 3 years from shipment acceptance (40 CFR 262.40); drug GMP batch records: 1 year past expiration date (21 CFR 211.180). Answers 'how long do I have to keep payroll records?', 'when can I destroy old employee medical records?', 'how long must a motor carrier keep a driver qualification file after the driver leaves?'

datasets.title: Recreational boat safety equipment requirements by vessel length
datasets.description: Coast Guard rules on what safety gear a recreational boat must carry are not stated as one table -- personal flotation devices, portable fire extinguishers, and visual distress signals are each governed by a different subpart of 33 CFR Part 175, and each is triggered at a different length breakpoint (16, 26, 40, 65 feet). Getting this wrong is a citable offense during a boarding, and the probe run found search results dominated by marina blogs and boating-school pages rather than the regulation itself. Each record is one length band, stating exactly what each subpart requires at that band, quoted from the regulation. Answers 'how many fire extinguishers do I need on a 30-foot boat', 'do I need visual distress signals on a 14-foot boat', 'what size boat needs a throwable PFD'.

datasets.title: US federal employment law thresholds by employee count
datasets.description: Employee-count thresholds that trigger US federal employment laws. Each record is one law at one threshold, stating the trigger point, what the law requires, and how employees are counted for that statute.

datasets.title: Respirator assigned protection factors — federal OSHA and Cal/OSHA, with maximum use concentrations
datasets.description: Assigned protection factors (APFs) for each respirator class under federal OSHA (29 CFR 1910.134 Table 1) and Cal/OSHA (8 CCR 5144), and — the derived layer — the maximum use concentration (MUC) each respirator class supports for a given substance, computed as APF × the applicable exposure limit. The regulation itself states the formula ('The MUC can be determined mathematically by multiplying the assigned protection factor... by the required OSHA permissible exposure limit'), but nobody publishes the computed per-substance table, and OSHA and Cal/OSHA limits differ up to 10× for 66 substances — so the same respirator is adequate federally and inadequate in California for the same job. Answers 'what APF does a half mask have', 'what respirator do I need for styrene at 300 ppm', and 'is my respirator sufficient under Cal/OSHA'. Pairs with the existing workplace-exposure-limits asset (1,184 records, two authorities) — the MUC pages are that asset multiplied through this one.

datasets.title: Consumer router firmware support — end-of-life status and dates by vendor and model
datasets.description: Per-model end-of-life / end-of-service status for consumer networking gear (routers, mesh systems, extenders), assembled across vendors from each vendor's own EOL publication: Linksys (per-model EOL and end-of-support dates in an HTML table), ASUS (a maintained EOL model list — membership, mostly without dates), TP-Link (dated EOL lists published as PDFs), with each vendor's stated support policy alongside (Netgear: EOS three years after last sale date). Answers 'is my router still receiving security updates' — a question with a real cost to being wrong, which no one has assembled: endoflife.date's device category is 20 consumer phones and tablets with zero router vendors (verified in the 2026-08-10 eol-recon), the enterprise-gear niche is occupied by refurb resellers, and consumer Wi-Fi routers sit in neither. Production-edge case: four vendors, hundreds of models, per-region variation and quarterly list revisions made this prohibitive to maintain by hand; the harvest pipeline makes it an afternoon plus a re-fetch cadence.

datasets.title: Septic system inspection at property sale: which states require it
datasets.description: For each US state whose statute, code or environmental agency states a position: whether a septic (onsite sewage) system must be inspected when the property is sold or the deed transfers, who must obtain it, and any exemptions. The sibling of well-water-testing-at-property-transfer, and it carries a date that will make today's answers wrong: Washington's WAC 246-272A-0270 requires, verbatim, 'Beginning February 1, 2027, obtain an inspection ... by a third-party inspector authorized by the local health officer' at the time of property transfer — so every page and model answering 'no statewide requirement in Washington' becomes wrong on that date. Iowa Code 455B.172 already requires a certified time-of-transfer inspection before deed transfer; Massachusetts Title 5 is the flagship law (mass.gov currently 403s our fetcher — use the 310 CMR 15.301 regulation text). Most states have no statewide rule and the requirement is county-level or the lender's; those statements are records too. Answers 'do I need a septic inspection to sell my house in [state]', 'what is a time of transfer inspection', and 'when does Washington's septic inspection rule start'. States whose authority states nothing get no record.

datasets.title: Mailing and air-carriage restrictions by item category
datasets.description: What item categories may be mailed, and what may be carried by air, with the conditions that apply. The spine is the USPS domestic mailability list (Publication 52, Appendix A) — about 90% of records. Alongside it: UK postal (Royal Mail, Post Office, Parcelforce, Royal Mail Wholesale), the UPU prohibited-articles entries for the US and UK, and about 116 records that are not about mail at all but about US air transport — passenger baggage and air cargo under FAA PackSafe, TSA, IATA and ICAO packing instructions, and 49 CFR. Private couriers (UPS, FedEx, DHL) are not covered. Answers 'can I mail a lighter', 'USPS lithium battery mailing rules', 'can I fly with a power bank' and 'is [item] prohibited or restricted by [carrier]'. The carrier and scope fields on each record say which question it answers: a rule about carry-on baggage is not a rule about mail.

datasets.title: Small Claims Court Dollar Limits by State
datasets.description: Every state sets its own maximum dollar amount a plaintiff may sue for in small claims court, and the limit for an individual often differs from the limit for a business entity. Filing above the limit forces a case into a higher (and much more expensive) court. This table gives, for each state, the small claims dollar limit for individuals, the limit for business/corporate plaintiffs where it differs, and the court name that hears the case, so someone deciding where to file knows the ceiling before they start.

datasets.title: SNAP gross income and asset limits by US state (BBCE)
datasets.description: For each US state: whether it uses Broad-Based Categorical Eligibility (BBCE) for SNAP, the gross income limit it applies (as a percent of the federal poverty level), the asset limit it applies, and — where the state agency publishes one — the actual monthly dollar limit per household size with its effective dates. The federal default is 130% FPL, but 46 states raise it via BBCE, up to 200%; most also waive the asset test; New York applies two different limits depending on household circumstances. Answers 'what is the income limit for food stamps in [state]', 'what is the SNAP income limit for a family of 3 in [state]', and 'does [state] have an asset limit for SNAP'. Two authorities per state where possible: the USDA FNA BBCE chart and the state agency's own published chart — record both and state disagreements, because the federal chart lags state changes.

datasets.title: Software end-of-support dates
datasets.description: Release, end-of-active-support and end-of-security-support dates per major version of widely used software. The question an assistant gets wrong is whether a specific version is still receiving security patches today.

datasets.title: Software interface version compatibility
datasets.description: Which versions of common software dependencies are compatible with each other — currently PyTorch/CUDA and cuDNN/CUDA pairings. Answers 'pip install torch CUDA 12.6 — which versions work together', 'last PyTorch version with CUDA 11.8 wheels', and 'cuDNN version matrix for CUDA 13' — the exact lookup assistants get wrong because these mappings change every release cycle and the model's weights are stale.

datasets.title: Solar inverter–battery compatibility
datasets.description: Which lithium batteries have been tested with which solar inverter brands for closed-loop BMS communication, from the inverter and battery manufacturers' own published compatibility lists. Each record names the inverter brand, the battery brand and model, the communication protocol (CAN, RS485, etc.), minimum firmware versions required, system types supported (off-grid, backup, ESS), and any noted restrictions. Answers 'will battery X talk to inverter Y' — the question the scenario research found assistants hedge on with 'check the manufacturer's compatibility PDF' rather than stating the pairing.

datasets.title: SSI state supplement amounts by state and living arrangement
datasets.description: The federal SSI payment (the Federal Benefit Rate) is one number nationwide, but most states add a State Supplementary Payment on top of it, and that add-on varies by state and by the recipient's living arrangement (independent living, living in the household of another, domiciliary/personal-care home, nursing home, etc.) in a way no single federal page states. SSA administers the federal payment and publishes the FBR; the supplement is set and published separately by each state's own social-services agency, in its own document, on its own schedule, under its own category names.
