A record here is one state's one living-arrangement category with the FBR, the state supplement amount, and the date the amount took effect. Answers 'how much is the SSI state supplement in Pennsylvania for someone in a personal care boarding home', 'does Michigan add anything to the federal SSI check for domiciliary care and how much', and 'why is my total SSI payment higher than the federal maximum'. Living-arrangement categories differ in name and count from state to state — record the category exactly as the state's own document names it rather than mapping it onto a shared taxonomy, since the mapping itself is where two states' 'domiciliary care' can mean different things.

datasets.title: State construction apprentice-to-journeyman ratio requirements by trade
datasets.description: Apprentice-to-journeyman ratio requirements for construction trades in each US state. Each record is one state and one trade or program, giving the initial ratio (how many journeymen for the first apprentice), the ratio thereafter (how many additional journeymen per additional apprentice), and whether it applies to public works, private, or both. Answers 'what is the apprentice-to-journeyman ratio for [trade] in [state]' and 'how many journeymen do I need before I can hire another apprentice on this job'. Ratios vary widely, and states structure them differently: some (MN) delegate to individual JATC programs, each with its own ratio; others (CA) set a state-wide hourly ratio on public works with trade-specific exemptions.

datasets.title: Certificate of need programs by US state
datasets.description: Which US states operate a certificate-of-need (CON) program for healthcare facilities, and what each program regulates. Each record is one state or DC: whether a CON program exists, which facility types and services are subject to review, whether any moratorium applies, and the statute citation. Answers 'does [state] require a certificate of need at all' and 'is [hospital beds / imaging equipment / an ambulatory surgery centre] reviewable in [state]'. Where NCSL's overview states a dollar trigger it is recorded here too, but it does so for only about half the CON states — for dollar thresholds read from each state's own statute, see con-capital-expenditure-thresholds-by-state.

datasets.title: Civil statute of limitations by state and type of claim
datasets.description: How long do you have to sue? Every state sets a different clock for each kind of civil claim, and missing it ends the claim outright — no defence, no appeal on the merits. The spread is wide and it moves: Florida cut its personal-injury period from four years to two in March 2023 (HB 837), Louisiana went the other way in July 2024, and a great many 'statute of limitations by state' tables still print the old figures. One record per state per type of claim — personal injury, medical malpractice, wrongful death, written contract, oral contract, property damage, fraud, defamation, debt — each quoted verbatim from that state's own legislature or revisor, never from a law-firm summary or a code mirror. The period is recorded in the statute's own words ('two years', 'six years'), not converted, because the conversion is where these tables go wrong. Answers 'statute of limitations for personal injury in Ohio', 'how long to sue for breach of contract by state', 'medical malpractice filing deadline', 'defamation statute of limitations'. Adjacent to state-construction-defect-limitations-periods, mechanics-lien-deadlines-by-state and whistleblower-filing-deadlines. This is a deadline lookup, not legal advice: tolling, discovery rules, minority, and claims against government bodies all change the answer, and the record says so where the statute does.

datasets.title: State construction defect statute of limitations and statute of repose periods
datasets.description: Can I still sue for this construction defect? Every US state sets two independent clocks: the statute of limitations (SOL — typically 2-6 years from discovery of the defect) and the statute of repose (SOR — typically 6-15 years from substantial completion, regardless of discovery). Both must be alive to file a claim. California gives 4 years SOL latent / 10 years SOR. Colorado gives 2 years SOL / 6 years SOR. New York has NO statute of repose for buildings. Getting this wrong means losing the right to file entirely. One record per state, sourced from the state's own statute. Answers 'construction defect statute of limitations by state', 'statute of repose for construction in Texas', 'how long can I sue for a building defect'. Adjacent to mechanics-lien-deadlines and construction-retainage-limits.

datasets.title: Consumer contract cooling-off and rescission periods by US state and transaction type
datasets.description: State-by-state comparison of the cancellation windows consumers have after signing specific types of contracts. Each record is one (state, transaction type) pair with the number of days the consumer has to cancel, the notice method required, refund timeline, and the statute citation. Covers transaction types that commonly carry cooling-off periods: home solicitation sales, health club memberships, timeshare purchases, extended warranties, hearing aid purchases, life insurance policies, dating/social referral services, credit repair services, membership travel, reverse mortgages, and door-to-door sales. The federal FTC cooling-off rule (16 CFR 429, 3 business days for door-to-door sales ≥$25) is the baseline; states add their own transaction types and periods on top. Answers 'how many days do I have to cancel a gym membership in [state]', 'what is the cooling-off period for timeshare purchases in [state]', and 'can I cancel this extended warranty'.

datasets.title: Dam safety hazard classification, inspection frequency, and owner obligations by US state
datasets.description: State-by-state comparison of dam safety programs: hazard classification systems, inspection frequencies, who must inspect, and dam owner obligations. Each record is one (state, hazard class) pair with the classification name, criteria for that class, required inspection interval, inspector qualifications, and whether inspections are mandatory or voluntary. Covers the ~91,000 non-federal dams in the US. Answers 'how often must my dam be inspected in [state]', 'what hazard classification is my dam', 'do I need a licensed engineer for inspections in [state]', and 'what are the penalties for non-compliance'. The ASDSO published a 50-state summary in 2020 as a PDF; it is now 6 years stale and not structured for search. This asset maintains the current state of each program from each state's own dam safety statute and program pages.

datasets.title: US state consumer data privacy laws: applicability thresholds by state
datasets.description: For each US state with a comprehensive consumer data privacy law, the thresholds a business must meet for the law to apply: consumer volume (number of state residents whose data is processed), revenue from data sales (percentage of gross revenue derived from selling personal data), revenue floor (minimum annual revenue), and whether these conditions are combined with AND or OR logic — sourced from the state's own statute. Answers 'does [state]'s privacy law apply to my business', 'what are the CCPA thresholds for 2026', 'which state privacy laws have no revenue threshold', 'how many consumers triggers the Virginia privacy law', 'which states changed their privacy law thresholds in 2026' (Connecticut lowers from 100k to 35k consumers on July 1, 2026, and adds a sensitive-data trigger with no volume floor; Indiana, Kentucky, and Rhode Island took effect January 1, 2026), 'which state has the lowest privacy law threshold' (Montana: 25k consumers), and 'does Utah require both a revenue AND consumer threshold' (yes — the only state using AND logic). As of mid-2026, 20 states have comprehensive consumer privacy laws in effect. No single authority publishes the thresholds for all states — each state's statute defines its own — which is why assembled versions come from compliance-software vendors (Feroot, IAPP, MultiState, PrivacyLawMap). The thresholds spread is wide: consumer volume from 25k (Montana) to 175k (Tennessee); revenue percentage from 0% (Texas, no numeric threshold) to 50% (Virginia model); revenue floor from $0 to $26.6M (California, inflation-adjusted). The AND/OR distinction matters: most states use OR (any threshold triggers the law), while Utah requires both revenue AND consumer volume, and Connecticut (CA) requires meeting one of three distinct paths.

datasets.title: State Earned Wage Access (EWA) Regulatory Frameworks — Classification, Fee Caps, and Licensing Requirements
datasets.description: How is earned wage access regulated in each state? Twelve states have enacted EWA-specific laws as of March 2026, with wide variation: some classify EWA as a loan requiring a consumer lending license, others create a new product category exempt from lending laws. This dataset records each state's product classification, fee caps, licensing or registration requirements, consumer protections, enforcement provisions, and statutory citations.

datasets.title: State controlled-substance scheduling of xylazine and tianeptine
datasets.description: For each US state that has acted, the controlled-substance schedule it assigns to substances that are NOT federally scheduled: xylazine and tianeptine — sourced from the state's own statute or administrative rule. Answers 'is tianeptine legal in [state]', 'is xylazine a controlled substance in [state]', and 'what schedule is tianeptine in [state]'. Control is entirely state-by-state, it is moving fast (states acted 2023–2026), and crucially the schedule is NOT the same everywhere: tianeptine is Schedule I in Florida, Georgia, Virginia, Minnesota, Delaware and Ohio but Schedule II in Tennessee, North Carolina and Nebraska, and xylazine is Schedule I in Florida, Schedule III in Delaware, Ohio, Nebraska and South Carolina, and Schedule IV in West Virginia. The only cross-state assemblies are a March-2024 PDF (LAPPA, xylazine only) and citation-free listicles. Kratom generally, 7-hydroxymitragynine (controlled federally by DEA temporary order from 2026, and at state level through kratom-product laws rather than schedules) and delta-8 are out of scope — seller sites cover them comprehensively. A state whose instrument cannot be confirmed on a fetched page is omitted, not guessed.

datasets.title: State employment law headcount triggers that deviate from federal thresholds
datasets.description: Employee-count thresholds at which state-specific employment laws kick in, focusing on where states deviate from the federal floor. Each record is one state and one law category (mini-COBRA, mini-WARN, state anti-discrimination, state family leave, workers compensation), giving the state's threshold, the federal threshold for comparison, how they differ, and the statute citation. Answers 'at how many employees does [state law] start applying in [state]' and 'does [state] have a mini-COBRA / mini-WARN / state family leave law'. Companion to the existing regulatory-threshold-triggers asset which covers federal thresholds only.

datasets.title: State insurance mandates for fertility treatment and IVF coverage
datasets.description: Which US states require private health insurers to cover fertility diagnosis, treatment, or preservation, and the specific terms of each mandate. Each record is one state, stating the mandate type (treatment, preservation only, or offer/cover distinction), which treatments are covered (IVF, GIFT, ZIFT, fertility preservation), cycle or dollar limits, age restrictions, employer-size thresholds, self-insured plan exemption status, religious employer exemption, effective date, and the statute citation. As of 2026, 25 states plus DC require some form of fertility coverage, but the variation is enormous: California (SB 729, effective January 2026) mandates IVF in large group plans with no cycle limit; Arkansas caps lifetime coverage at $15,000 and requires trying cheaper treatments first; Delaware covers six egg retrievals but only for iatrogenic infertility; several states mandate only fertility preservation for cancer patients. Self-insured employer plans (covering ~65% of workers with job-based insurance) are exempt from all state mandates under federal ERISA. Answers 'does my state require insurance to cover IVF', 'how many IVF cycles does my state mandate', 'does the fertility mandate apply to my employer', and 'what are the age limits for mandated fertility coverage in [state]'.

datasets.title: State Heat Illness Prevention Standards — Temperature Triggers and Required Employer Actions
datasets.description: At what outdoor temperature must employers provide shade, water, rest breaks, and written prevention plans? Six U.S. states enforce specific heat illness prevention standards with temperature triggers that exceed the stalled federal OSHA proposal. This dataset compares each state's trigger temperatures, required actions at each tier, coverage scope (indoor/outdoor, which industries), acclimatization requirements, and regulatory citations.

datasets.title: State Insurance Department Complaint Index by Company
datasets.description: Every state insurance department publishes, for each licensed insurer and line of business, how many complaints consumers filed against that company and how much premium the company wrote in that state, together with its own summary figure comparing the two. Nobody publishes it across states. Each regulator uses its own file format, its own line-of-business names, its own schedule — and, the part that catches people out, its own arithmetic. Indiana's "Complaint Index" is the company's share of all complaints divided by its share of all premium written in Indiana, so 1.00 is the state average. Michigan's "Complaint Ratio" is complaints per $1 million of written premium, which is a different quantity on a different scale with no meaning at 1.00. Putting those two in one column without saying so would get the asset's whole point wrong. So every record here carries the complaint count and the premium alongside the state's published figure, and quotes the state's own heading for that figure. The raw counts compare across states; the summary figures do not.

datasets.title: State insurer-of-last-resort programs — FAIR Plan / Citizens eligibility and coverage limits
datasets.description: When private insurers won't write a property in a wildfire or hurricane state, the state's residual-market insurer (a FAIR Plan or a corporation like Florida's Citizens) is the fallback — but the dollar limits and the rule that determines who is even eligible differ by state and are stated only in that state's own statute or program announcement. Each record is one state's program, carrying its coverage-category limit and, where the source states one, the rule that makes a property ineligible. Answers 'what's the maximum FAIR Plan payout in California', 'why would Florida Citizens turn down my house', 'which states cap eligibility by a dollar replacement-cost figure vs. a pricing-comparison rule'.

datasets.title: State lemon law eligibility thresholds: time limits, mileage, and repair attempts by US state
datasets.description: When does a car qualify as a lemon in your state? The thresholds that trigger a state lemon law vary widely: the qualifying window runs from one year or 12,000 miles (Illinois) and one year or 15,000 miles (Massachusetts) to two years or 24,000 miles (Arizona, Texas); repair attempts that raise the presumption range from 2 (serious safety defects in Washington and California) to 4; days out of service run from 15 business days (Massachusetts) to 30 days, counted as calendar days in some states and business days in others. One record per state, quoted from the state attorney general's consumer page where reachable and from the state statute itself where the AG page blocks non-browser fetches — most do (7 of 10 AG pages tried returned 403/404/500), so assistants answer these questions from training data rather than current statute, and lemon laws do change. Answers 'is my car a lemon in California', 'how many repair attempts before lemon law applies', 'what is the mileage limit for lemon law in Texas', and 'lemon law requirements by state'.

datasets.title: State health insurance marketplace assistance by state: who runs it, where subsidies start and stop, and what the state adds
datasets.description: One record per US state and the District of Columbia, stating who operates its health insurance marketplace, the income at which premium tax credit eligibility begins there, whether a coverage gap exists below it, and what the state itself adds on top of the federal credit. When the ACA's enhanced premium tax credits lapsed on 31 December 2025 a group of states stood up or expanded their own premium assistance to absorb part of the loss, and they did so on completely different terms: New Mexico backfills the full loss below 400% of the poverty line and caps benchmark premiums at 8.5% of income above it; New Jersey's assistance runs to 600% of the poverty line; Maryland covers the whole loss below 200% and part of it to 400%; California stops at 165%; Colorado pays a flat monthly amount; Washington pays per member per month. In ten states that never adopted the Medicaid expansion, a household below the poverty line still qualifies for nothing at all. Whether the federal cutoff at 400% of the poverty line is a cliff or a slope therefore depends entirely on the state, and no page states the answer for all fifty-one. Answers 'does my state have its own health insurance subsidy', 'what is the income limit for marketplace insurance in [state]', 'am I in the coverage gap', and 'does [state] have a health insurance mandate'. Open enrollment dates are deliberately not carried. The 2027 window is legally unsettled -- a June 2026 ruling vacated the federal rule that would have shortened it, an appeal was open, and the marketplaces' own pages describe their 2027 dates as expected or currently scheduled rather than fixed. A YYYY-MM-DD field cannot carry that hedge, so the dates are omitted rather than published as settled; healthcare.gov and each marketplace state them directly.

datasets.title: State mini-WARN act thresholds: layoff notice requirements beyond federal WARN
datasets.description: For each US state with its own layoff-notice (mini-WARN) statute: the employer size that makes the law apply, the layoff or closing size that triggers notice, how many days of notice are owed, and whether severance is mandatory — each from the state's own statute with a verbatim quote. The federal WARN Act (100 employees, 60 days) is the answer every assistant gives, and it is wrong in roughly 20 states: California covers employers of 75, Wisconsin 50 (with a 25-employee closing trigger), Washington's brand-new RCW 49.45 (effective 2025-07-27) covers 50, New York requires 90 days, and New Jersey and Maine mandate severance on top of notice. Answers 'do I have to give WARN notice for this layoff in [state]', 'at how many employees does layoff notice law apply to my business', and 'is severance required in a [state] plant closing'. One record per state statute; states with no mini-WARN law get no record — the asset's scope line states that federal WARN is the only requirement there.

datasets.title: State Opioid Initial Prescribing Limits
datasets.description: Maximum days' supply for a first opioid prescription for acute pain, by state, with the statutory or regulatory citation. Over half the states cap initial prescriptions at 3 to 14 days; some also cap daily dosage in morphine milligram equivalents (MME).

datasets.title: State OSHA plan civil penalty maximums by violation type compared with federal
datasets.description: Maximum civil penalty amounts for workplace safety violations in each OSHA-approved State Plan, compared with the federal OSHA baseline. Each record is one state-plan jurisdiction and one violation type (serious, willful, repeat, other-than-serious, failure-to-abate, regulatory/posting). Gives the state's maximum and minimum penalty, the corresponding federal amount, and key structural differences in how the penalty is computed (severity tiers, employer-size reductions, good-faith adjustments). Answers 'what is the maximum fine for a serious OSHA violation in [state]' and 'how does [state]'s penalty structure differ from federal OSHA'. Special note for 2026: the October 2025 CPI-U was not produced due to the government shutdown, so federal penalties were not adjusted — but some state plans (CA, OR) adjusted independently, widening the gap.

datasets.title: State paid family and medical leave program contribution rates, benefits, and eligibility
datasets.description: The mandatory paid family and medical leave programs that US states operate, with each state's current contribution rate, employer/employee split, maximum weekly benefit, wage replacement formula, leave duration, covered reasons, employer-size threshold, and program launch date. As of mid-2026, 14 states plus DC operate programs: California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, DC, Maine, Massachusetts, Minnesota, New Jersey, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, and Washington. Maryland and Virginia have enacted programs launching in 2028. Contribution rates change annually (Washington rose to 1.13% for 2026; Massachusetts remains at 0.88%). Wage replacement ranges from a flat 67% (New York) to sliding scales giving 90-100% to low-wage workers (Washington, Oregon, Colorado, Minnesota). Duration ranges from 6 weeks (California family-only) to 26 weeks (Massachusetts military family). This is a production-edge asset: maintaining current rates across 15+ annually-changing programs was prohibitive for one person and is now economic. Answers 'what is the paid family leave contribution rate in [state]', 'how much paid leave do employees get in [state]', 'does my state have paid family leave', and 'what is the maximum paid leave benefit in [state]'.

datasets.title: US state paid family and medical leave (PFML) program requirements for employers
datasets.description: Contribution rates, employer/employee splits, employee-count thresholds, benefit durations, wage replacement formulas, and maximum weekly benefits for every US state that mandates paid family and medical leave. Each record is one state's PFML program, stating the current payroll contribution rate, who pays what share, when the program took effect, and the key compliance numbers an employer needs. Answers 'does my state require paid family leave', 'what is the PFML contribution rate in [state]', and 'how many weeks of paid leave do employees get in [state]'.

datasets.title: State pay transparency laws — salary range disclosure requirements
datasets.description: Whether an employer must disclose a salary/wage range in a job posting varies by state on three axes that only the statute text states precisely: the employee-count threshold that triggers the duty, whether the range must appear in the posting itself or only on request, and the penalty for non-compliance. Each record is one state, carrying its statutory citation, the employee-count threshold, what must be disclosed, and the penalty range. Answers 'does a 10-person company in New York have to post a salary range', 'what's the penalty for not disclosing pay in a Washington job posting', 'which states require pay-scale disclosure at 15 employees vs 4'.

datasets.title: US state PFAS product restriction effective dates by category
datasets.description: State-by-state PFAS product ban and restriction effective dates. Each record is one state’s ban on one product category, with the effective date, the statute or bill number, the enforcement agency, and any exemptions (e.g. currently unavoidable use). Answers 'can I sell [product] containing PFAS in [state] after [date]', 'which states ban PFAS in cookware', 'when does [state] ban all PFAS products'. Roughly 30 jurisdictions with active or pending PFAS product restrictions as of mid-2026, each with different product category definitions and phase-in schedules.

datasets.title: State prevailing wage law applicability thresholds
datasets.description: At what project dollar amount does the prevailing wage apply in each state? About 28 US states have their own prevailing wage laws ('Little Davis-Bacon Acts') covering state- and locally-funded construction. The threshold ranges from $0 (New York, Illinois — all public works) to $1,000 (California) to $500,000 (Colorado) to $1,000,000 (Connecticut new construction). The remaining ~22 states have no prevailing wage law. The federal Davis-Bacon Act applies to all federally-funded construction over $2,000 regardless of state. One record per state, sourced from that state's department of labor. Answers 'does prevailing wage apply to my project in Texas', 'what is the prevailing wage threshold in California', 'which states have prevailing wage laws', and 'do I have to pay prevailing wage on a $50,000 state project'. The DOL published the definitive comparison at dol.gov but it returns 403 to non-browser fetchers, so agents and assistants are locked out of the federal reference.

datasets.title: State tuition-free college (promise) programs: eligibility rules by state
datasets.description: For each US state with a statewide tuition-free college ('promise' or 'reconnect') program: the program name, which institutions and credentials it covers, the funding model (last-dollar vs first-dollar, as the page states it), the income limit if any, the age or cohort restriction (recent graduates vs adults 25+), residency requirements, and renewal conditions (credits, GPA, continuous enrollment). Answers 'is community college free in [state]', 'do I qualify for [state]'s free tuition program', and 'does [state]'s promise program cover a bachelor's degree'. Production-edge candidate: roughly 35 programs, each defined by its own statute and agency rules, changing yearly (Massachusetts's MassEducate started fall 2024; Colorado Promise is a tax-credit mechanism unlike any neighbour) — a table nobody maintains because by-hand upkeep across 35 legislatures was prohibitive. No single original exists: the College Promise catalog is an annual PDF report, and page one is scholarship content mills (scholarships360, collegefinance, degreecalc) with no comprehensive current comparison. One authority per record: the state higher-ed agency or the administering college system's own page. The fact/advice split matters here: which program exists, who qualifies, what it covers are facts; 'should I enroll' is not our product.

datasets.title: State public works payment and performance bond thresholds (Little Miller Acts)
datasets.description: Do I need a surety bond on this public works project in my state, and how much? Every US state has a 'Little Miller Act' requiring performance and/or payment bonds on public construction contracts, but the dollar thresholds, bond percentages, notice requirements, and claim deadlines differ in every state. California requires bonds on all public works contracts (no minimum) with payment bonds over $25,000. Texas requires bonds over $100,000 for state entities, $25,000 for payment bonds. Washington allows retainage in lieu of bond under $150,000. One record per state, sourced from the state's own statute. Answers 'Little Miller Act thresholds by state', 'do I need a bond on a $75,000 public project in Virginia', 'state payment bond requirements for construction'. Adjacent to mechanics-lien-deadlines, construction-retainage-limits, and construction-prompt-payment-deadlines.

datasets.title: State Residential Radon Disclosure, Testing, and Certification Requirements
datasets.description: State laws governing radon in residential real estate transactions vary dramatically. Some states require sellers to disclose known radon test results (Florida, Illinois, New Jersey). Others fold radon into broader environmental hazard disclosure forms (California, Colorado). Some mandate that radon measurement professionals be certified or licensed; others have no licensing requirement. EPA recommends 4 pCi/L as the action level but this is not a legal standard — state action levels may differ. This table gives the disclosure requirement, testing mandate, professional certification requirement, action level, and statute citation for each state.

datasets.title: State Right-to-Repair Laws: Coverage, Requirements, and Effective Dates
datasets.description: Which US states have enacted right-to-repair laws, what products each law covers (electronics, agricultural equipment, powered wheelchairs, automobiles), the price threshold above which parts and documentation must be provided, whether parts-pairing is prohibited, the enforcement mechanism (state AG only vs. private right of action), penalty amounts, and the effective date. As of August 2026, at least 8 states have enacted laws and 28+ have pending legislation.

datasets.title: State conformity to federal Section 179 and bonus depreciation rules
datasets.description: Whether each US state conforms to the federal Section 179 expensing limit and the 100% bonus depreciation deduction, and what state-specific caps or add-back rules apply when it does not. Each record is one state, stating its conformity status for both Section 179 and bonus depreciation, the state's own Section 179 dollar cap if different from federal, whether the state requires a bonus depreciation add-back, the depreciation method the state uses instead, and a statute or administrative citation. The federal Section 179 limit for 2026 is $2,560,000 with a $4,090,000 phase-out; 100% bonus depreciation was made permanent by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (January 2025). At least a dozen states decouple from bonus depreciation (California, New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Massachusetts, DC, Connecticut, Maryland, Tennessee, North Carolina, Indiana, Wisconsin among others), and several cap Section 179 far below the federal limit (California: $25,000; New Jersey: $25,000; Pennsylvania: not allowed for corporate income tax). A $480,000 equipment purchase in California produces roughly $51,000 in extra state tax in year one. Answers 'does my state allow bonus depreciation', 'what is the Section 179 limit in [state]', 'do I have to add back bonus depreciation on my state return', and 'which states decouple from federal depreciation rules'.

datasets.title: State small estate affidavit and simplified probate thresholds
datasets.description: Dollar thresholds below which heirs can use a small estate affidavit or simplified probate procedure to transfer a decedent's property without full probate, for each US state and DC. Each record is one jurisdiction, giving the personal property threshold for the affidavit procedure, any separate real property threshold, waiting period, whether a will is required to be absent, inflation adjustment schedule, and statute citation. Answers 'what is the small estate limit in [state]' and 'can I avoid probate for a $X estate in [state]'. Thresholds range from $5,000 (some states) to $208,850 (California, inflation-adjusted triennially). Several states adjust periodically; most do not. No existing compilation cites the underlying statutes, making verification impossible.

datasets.title: State unemployment insurance taxable wage bases and new employer tax rates by US state
datasets.description: For each US state and DC, the taxable wage base (the per-employee annual earnings cap on which unemployment insurance tax is owed) and the tax rate assigned to new employers — sourced from each state's labor department or employment security agency. Answers 'what is the unemployment tax wage base in [state]', 'what UI rate do new employers pay in [state]', 'SUTA wage base by state 2026', and 'state unemployment insurance taxable wage base comparison'. The federal FUTA wage base is $7,000 and has not changed since 1983, but states range from $7,000 (California, several others) to over $78,000 (Washington), a 10× difference in the tax base for the same employee. New employer rates also vary widely. Changes take effect annually and states announce at different times (some January 1, some July 1, some fiscal year). No existing source cross-references all 50 states with per-state citations to the actual .gov announcement.

datasets.title: US state unclaimed property dormancy periods by property type
datasets.description: How many years of inactivity before each type of property (wages, checks, insurance proceeds, utility deposits, gift cards, safe-deposit boxes, securities, etc.) must be reported as unclaimed in each US state. Each record is one state + property type with the dormancy period in years, the statute citation, and any conditions (e.g. dual thresholds for solids, different rules for government-held funds). Answers 'how long before uncashed payroll in [state] is escheatable?', 'what is the dormancy period for life insurance in [state]?', and 'which states have the shortest dormancy for [property type]?' — questions where the answer varies by state AND property type, and where getting it wrong triggers penalties and audit exposure.

datasets.title: US state universal occupational license recognition laws — conditions and scope
datasets.description: Which US states have passed universal occupational license recognition laws, what conditions they impose (minimum years licensed, good standing, criminal background, exam requirements), which professions are excluded, and whether military spouse provisions are included. Each record is one state's law with its specific conditions. Answers 'does [state] recognize my out-of-state professional license?', 'how long do I need to have been licensed to qualify?', 'are there professions excluded from universal recognition in [state]?', and 'does [state] have a military spouse licensing provision?' — questions where the answer is rapidly changing as states adopt new laws (22+ states as of mid-2026), and where the conditions differ meaningfully between states.

datasets.title: State Worker Classification Tests — Independent Contractor vs Employee
datasets.description: Which legal test each U.S. state uses to distinguish employees from independent contractors (ABC test, common law/right-to-control, or modified ABC), the statutory citation, key exemptions by industry or occupation, and the date the current test took effect.

datasets.title: Stihl chainsaw chain and bar specifications by model
datasets.description: Chain pitch, gauge, drive link count, bar length and OEM chain part number for each Stihl chainsaw model and bar combination. One row per model per bar length. Answers 'what chain does my Stihl MS261 take', 'Stihl MS440 20 inch bar drive links' and 'Stihl chain part number for [model]' — the multi-variable lookup assistants get wrong by guessing a plausible pitch/gauge combination.

datasets.title: Stolen EBT/SNAP benefit replacement policy by US state
datasets.description: For each US state that publishes one: whether SNAP or cash-assistance benefits stolen by electronic theft (skimming, cloning, phishing) are replaced, under what authority, and for what date ranges — after the federal replacement mandate expired on December 20, 2024. The answers now diverge sharply: New York stopped accepting SNAP replacement claims on September 30, 2025 while continuing Cash Assistance replacement; California responded with chip/tap card hardware for all 4.4M cardholders and warns benefits 'might not be replaced'. Every model trained before December 2024 asserts a federal replacement right that no longer exists. Answers 'my EBT benefits were stolen, will they be replaced in [state]', 'is there a deadline to claim stolen SNAP benefits', and 'does [state] replace skimmed cash assistance'. Only states whose agency states a policy get a record; no inference from silence.

datasets.title: Short-term rental registration rules, city by city, from each city's own page
datasets.description: For each major US city, from the city government's own page: whether short-term rentals must register or be licensed, the fee, the licence term, primary-residence and unit-count limits, and dated rule changes. This is the portfolio's first city-level asset — every other jurisdictional asset is state-level — and the rules are churning: Austin rewrote its rules three times in twelve months (Feb 2025 zoning change, Oct 2025 two-year licences and tenant operation, and from July 1, 2026 the city 'will begin requesting removal of unlicensed properties from STR platforms'); Chicago registers 'shared housing units' with $2,500–$10,000 fines per violation; NYC's Local Law 18 registration regime has a Prohibited Buildings List. The incumbents assembling this are property-management software vendors (Lodgify, Hospitable, Truvi) whose city guides are content marketing with no quotes, no dates and uneven freshness — keeping fifty city pages current by hand was the prohibitive part, and it is exactly what the pipeline does. Answers 'do I need a licence to Airbnb my place in [city]', 'what is the fine for an unregistered short-term rental in [city]', and 'what changed in [city]'s STR rules this year'. Cities whose page we cannot reach get no record.

datasets.title: Superseded and deprecated identifier mappings
datasets.description: Withdrawn standards, deprecated API models and retired identifiers mapped to their named successors. Answers 'what replaced X' when X is a standards document reference or an API model identifier — the exact lookup that assistants get confidently wrong on obscure designations.

datasets.title: Texas electrician licensing: practice questions with the answer quoted from TDLR
datasets.description: Practice questions on the Texas electrician licensing path — hours, supervision, application forms and fees, the exam, renewal, continuing education and reciprocity — where the answer to every question is a word-for-word extract from the page the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation publishes it on. This is NOT National Electrical Code practice. The Texas journeyman and master examinations are open-book NEC examinations and contain no questions on Texas law or TDLR rules at all, so nothing here rehearses exam content and no NEC text is reproduced. What it rehearses is everything around the exam, which is where applications actually fail: that 7,000 hours lets you sit the journeyman exam but 8,000 is required for the licence; that Journeyman Industrial experience cannot be used to qualify for Master; that hours from a career and technology education programme count for Residential Wireman and for nothing else; that a licence expired more than three years cannot be renewed at all. Answers 'how many hours to take the Texas journeyman electrician exam', 'Texas electrician license renewal fee', 'which states does Texas have electrician reciprocity with', 'how many CE hours for a Texas journeyman electrician' and 'what NEC edition is the Texas electrician exam'. The exam moves from the 2023 NEC to the 2026 NEC on 1 September 2026 and both statements are recorded here from the pages that make them.

datasets.title: Thermocouple type letter to alloy pair, ANSI/IEC color code and tolerance class
datasets.description: A thermocouple's type letter (J, K, T, E, N, R, S, B, C...) names an alloy pair, but the wire color that identifies it on the bench is set by a different standards body depending on where the part was made or bought — ANSI/ASTM MC96.1 uses one color code, IEC 60584-3 (and JIS C 1602 in Japan) uses a different one for the same alloy pair, and the two schemes disagree on which color means positive. Nobody publishes the type letter, both color codes, the alloy pair and the accuracy tolerance class on one page; a buyer or field technician instead has to hold two vendor charts side by side and hope the type letters line up. A record here is one thermocouple type with its positive/negative alloy names, ANSI positive/negative wire color, IEC positive/negative wire color, usable temperature range, and its ASTM E230 standard/special-limits tolerance alongside its IEC 60584-2 / JIS C 1602 class 1/2/3 tolerance. Answers 'is red positive or negative on a type K thermocouple', 'what color is IEC type J versus ANSI type J', 'what's the accuracy tolerance on a class 2 type N thermocouple', and 'my probe has a yellow and red wire, what type is it and is that ANSI or IEC'.

datasets.title: TLS certificate and CA requirement effective dates (CA/Browser Forum, Chrome, Mozilla)
datasets.description: Forward-dated schedule of when each TLS certificate and certificate authority requirement takes effect, and which programme it binds. Each record is one requirement with its effective date, the Baseline Requirements section it amends, and the authority imposing it. Covers the CA/Browser Forum TLS Baseline Requirements effective-date table, the Google Chrome Root Program policy, and the Mozilla Root Store Policy. Answers 'when does the 200 day certificate lifetime take effect', 'TLS certificate maximum validity 100 days date', '47 day certificates 2029 timeline', 'when does domain validation reuse drop to 200 days', 'SC-081 phased schedule', and 'when do CAs have to do DNSSEC validation'. The dates changed recently and change again with every ballot, so an answer from model memory describes a world that has already moved; the maximum subscriber certificate validity drops to 200 days on 2026-03-15 and to 100 days on 2027-03-15, and the domain-validation reuse period and the subject-identity reuse period fall on different schedules to each other.

datasets.title: Toll transponder interoperability: which pass works in which states
datasets.description: For each US toll transponder programme (E-ZPass, SunPass and SunPass PRO, TxTag and the Central US partners, and the rest as their pages prove reachable): the states and networks where that transponder is accepted, from the operating agency's own interoperability page with a verbatim quote. No authority maintains the national matrix — the E-ZPass Group's member list sits behind an agency login, and the only assembled versions are toll-calculator vendors' blog posts. The answers cross-cut: SunPass PRO works on E-ZPass roads in 19 states but the plain SunPass Mini works in only six; a TxTag works in Kansas and Oklahoma but not on E-ZPass roads; Florida's Turnpike accepts E-ZPass but only via specific transponder models. Answers 'will my E-ZPass work in Florida', 'which toll pass should I get for a Texas-to-Chicago drive', and 'does SunPass work in Georgia'. One record per transponder-programme statement of acceptance, quoting the agency page.

datasets.title: Maximum legal vehicle size and weight limits by US state
datasets.description: For each US state, the maximum legal dimensions and gross weight a vehicle plus load may have on state highways before an oversize/overweight permit is required, from the state's own vehicle code or DOT/DMV page: width, height, semitrailer length, combination length, and gross weight. Height genuinely fragments — 13 feet 6 inches in most eastern states (Florida, Ohio), 14 feet in western states (Washington) — so a load legal in one state needs a permit in the next. Answers 'how tall can a truck be in [state]', 'what is the maximum legal trailer length in [state]', and 'at what point do I need an oversize permit in [state]'. Values verbatim from statute or the agency page; the many exceptions (auto transporters, safety devices, RVs) stay in the source quote, not in extra fields.

datasets.title: EPA TSCA Section 6 chemical risk management status: prohibitions, effective dates, and exemptions
datasets.description: Status of EPA risk management rules for chemicals found to present unreasonable risk under TSCA Section 6. Each record is one chemical with its current rule status (proposed/final/effective), effective dates for prohibitions, specific uses prohibited, and any exemptions or compliance date extensions. Currently covers ~11 chemicals under Section 6(a) active risk management plus 5 PBT chemicals under Section 6(h). The pipeline has 20+ more chemicals in risk evaluation. Answers 'is [chemical] being regulated under TSCA?', 'when does the prohibition on methylene chloride take effect?', 'which uses of TCE are exempt?', and 'what is the current rule status for 1-bromopropane?'

datasets.title: Unemployment insurance: maximum weekly benefit and weeks of duration by US state
datasets.description: For each US state: the maximum (and minimum, where stated) weekly unemployment benefit amount, the maximum number of payable weeks, and — where the state uses one — the sliding-scale rule that ties duration to the state unemployment rate. Answers 'how much is unemployment in [state]', 'how many weeks of unemployment can I get in [state]', and 'what is the maximum unemployment benefit in [state]'. The claimant-side counterpart to the employer-side wage-base asset proposed 2026-08-17. The confident-wrong conditions are strong: Texas's cap moved from $591 to $605 in October 2025 (indexed annually, so any trained-in figure decays every October); several states no longer offer the 'standard' 26 weeks (NC and FL are at 12, tied to the unemployment rate by formula), and page one is entirely content mills (savingtoinvest, layoffcalc, remotelaws) — the DOL comparison of state UI laws is an annual PDF, not an agent-reachable page. One authority per record: the state workforce agency's own page or the state statute. Record the duration formula verbatim where one exists — the formula is the fact that generic answers flatten.

datasets.title: UL-Classified replacement circuit breaker cross-reference by panel brand
datasets.description: Residential circuit breakers that Underwriters Laboratories has Classified for use in a different manufacturer's load centre, taken from each manufacturer's own catalog. Each record is one classified breaker: its own catalog number, its ampere rating, and the competing brands' breakers it is listed to replace. Answers 'my panel is a Square D and the supply house only has Eaton in stock — what fits'. There is no single public database of this because UL Classification is tested breaker-by-breaker and every manufacturer publishes only its own outbound mapping, never the full grid across competitors.

datasets.title: Underground Storage Tank Operator Training Requirements by State
datasets.description: Training, certification, and renewal requirements for Class A, B, and C UST operators in each US state, including whether EPA online training is accepted, exam pass thresholds, renewal intervals, and the implementing agency.

datasets.title: Winter utility shutoff/disconnection moratorium by state
datasets.description: Whether a utility can disconnect service for non-payment during winter, and under what conditions, varies by state on the exact season window, which utility types are covered, and whether an income test applies. Existing free summaries (e.g. energy-broker lead-gen sites) round this to 'most cold states ban Dec-Mar disconnects', which is not precise enough to answer a specific household's situation. Each record is one state and one class of utility — several states set a different window or income test for water than for electric and gas — carrying the exact moratorium window, covered utility types, and eligibility/income test if any, sourced from the state's own regulation or utility-commission order rather than a secondary summary. Answers 'can my gas get shut off in January in Pennsylvania', 'does New Jersey's winter shutoff protection cover water bills', 'what income level qualifies for winter shutoff protection in my state'.

datasets.title: Miele vacuum cleaner bag type by model series
datasets.description: Which Miele dust bag type (GN, FJM, U, or KK) fits a given Miele vacuum cleaner model series. Answers 'which bag do I need for my Miele vacuum?'

datasets.title: Vehicle emissions testing: which counties require it, in which states
datasets.description: For each US state that runs a vehicle emissions inspection (I/M) program: which counties require testing, how often, which vehicles are exempt, and the test type — from the state environmental agency's own page, not a DMV content mill. The answer is county-level, not state-level, and it is moving: North Carolina asked EPA to remove all nineteen of its remaining counties (submitted October 2024), Texas is adding Bexar County (San Antonio) in 2026, and Colorado is changing test types in 2026. Georgia's program covers exactly 13 named metro-Atlanta counties; Texas covers 17 counties across four metros; Colorado covers all or part of 9 Front Range counties; California's list of 34 counties is the fact that testing there is not statewide. Some exemptions move on their own: Virginia's regulation exempts anything older than 'the current calendar year minus 24', so the cut-off year advances every January whether or not anyone republishes the page; Vermont tests the OBD system on vehicles '16 model years old or newer', and New York's OBDII window runs from 'the current year minus 25' to 'the current year minus two' — three rolling cut-offs no static listicle tracks. The north-east answers the county question differently: Vermont, New Jersey, Rhode Island, Delaware and New Hampshire inspect everywhere in the state, and in New York the county list that matters is the Diesel Emissions Metropolitan Area for heavy diesels, while light diesels take the OBDII test anywhere in the state. EPA maintains no current state/county list — only technical guidance. Utah is the clearest case for asking the question county by county: its program is run by five county health departments and they do not share one rule, so Cache County exempts vehicles less than six model years old while Salt Lake, Davis, Weber and Utah counties test them every other year, and Utah County alone tests 1998–2021 diesels. New Mexico's whole program is one county — Bernalillo — under the Albuquerque-Bernalillo County Air Quality Control Board's own regulation. Two states are recorded here as stated absences rather than omitted: Idaho repealed the state I/M requirement effective 1 July 2023, and EPA removed Tennessee's six counties from the federally-approved plan effective 16 September 2021 — though that rule's own footnote says it does not preclude counties keeping a local program, so 'Tennessee has no testing' is not quite what the source says. Two gaps are stated rather than papered over. Ohio names no county anywhere we can reach: OAC 3745-26-01(G) defines the program area by nonattainment status instead of by name, so the cadence, the twenty-five-year scope, the exemptions and the E-Check contract's June 2027 end date are recorded and the county list is not claimed. And Massachusetts carries no cadence, because the annual interval lives in 540 CMR 4.00, which no host that will serve us publishes as text; its scope and exemptions come from Cornell LII's mirror of 310 CMR 60.02 — a mirror, not mass.gov, which blocks us, and one that states it reflects amendments only through 11 August 2017. Answers 'do I need an emissions test to register my car in [county], [state]', 'is [state] getting rid of emissions testing', and 'how old does my car have to be to be exempt in [state]'. States with no program get no record unless their agency states the absence.

datasets.title: Vehicle inspection defect categories: MOT major, minor and dangerous verdicts
datasets.description: What each vehicle defect is categorised as at a roadworthiness inspection, and therefore whether it fails the test. Each record is one defect under one authority, stating the defect reference, the defect wording as published, and the category (Minor, Major or Dangerous). Covers the DVSA MOT inspection manual for cars, vans and passenger vehicles (classes 3, 4, 5 and 7), the DVSA MOT inspection manual for motorcycles (classes 1 and 2), EU Directive 2014/45/EU Annex I, and the US minimum periodic inspection standards in 49 CFR Appendix A to Part 396. Answers 'is a cracked windscreen a major or minor MOT defect', 'MOT inspection manual zone A windscreen damage', 'does a worn wheel bearing fail an MOT', 'is a tyre bulge dangerous or major', and 'what fails an MOT test'. The same defect usually appears twice, once Major and once Dangerous, separated only by a severity qualifier, and the UK, EU and US verdicts for the same physical fault do not always agree.

datasets.title: Vehicle title transfer deadlines and late penalties by state
datasets.description: For each US state: how many days a private-party buyer has to apply for a new certificate of title after buying a vehicle, and what the statute charges for missing the deadline — each from the state's own titling statute with a verbatim quote. There is no federal rule and the answers spread from 10 days (California, Minnesota's notice-of-sale) through 15 (Washington) to 30 (Texas, Ohio, Florida), and the penalties are just as scattered: Florida a flat $20, Washington $50 on the sixteenth day plus $2 for each additional day capped at $125, Texas escalating to $250. Answers 'how long do I have to transfer a car title after buying in [state]', 'what is the penalty for late title transfer in [state]', and 'is there a late fee if I miss the title deadline'. The Washington and Texas penalty formulas are stated as day-rate schedules, so a late-penalty calculator (inputs: state, days late) falls straight out of the data. One record per state statute.

datasets.title: Vehicle trade-in sales tax credit rules by state -- full price taxed, or only the difference
datasets.description: When you trade a car in, does the state charge sales tax on the full price of the new car, or only on the price left after the trade-in is deducted? On a $40,000 car with a $15,000 trade-in, that choice is about $900 in a 6% state. This covers 47 states, each taken from that state's own Department of Revenue, DMV or statute, with the sentence that states the rule quoted on every record.  Most states deduct the trade-in in full. Four charge tax on the whole price: California, Virginia, Oklahoma and Oregon. Four allow the deduction only in part, and these are the ones commonly reported wrongly -- Michigan caps it in dollars, Ohio allows it on new vehicles but not used, Georgia allows it on dealer sales but not private-party sales, and Rhode Island allows it on passenger vehicles, motorcycles and motor homes only. Alaska, Delaware and Montana charge no state sales tax on a vehicle at all.  The District of Columbia, Hawaii, Mississippi and New Hampshire are not covered: no official page for those states states a trade-in rule we could quote.

datasets.title: State Property Tax Exemptions for Disabled Veterans — Exemption Amounts, Disability Rating Thresholds, and Eligibility Rules
datasets.description: How much property tax does a disabled veteran owe in each state? All 50 states offer some form of property tax exemption for veterans with service-connected disabilities, but the exemption amount, qualifying disability rating, home value caps, and surviving spouse provisions vary enormously. This dataset records each state's exemption type, dollar amounts or percentage thresholds by disability rating level, home value limits, surviving spouse eligibility, annual adjustment mechanism, and the specific statutory citation.

datasets.title: VOC content limits for architectural coatings by jurisdiction
datasets.description: Maximum volatile organic compound (VOC) content limits for architectural coatings (paint, primer, stain, sealant, varnish) by regulatory jurisdiction. Each record is one coating category under one jurisdiction, stating the VOC limit in grams per liter and the effective date. Covers US federal (40 CFR 59 Subpart D), SCAQMD Rule 1113, California CARB SCM, OTC Model Rule (NY, NJ and others), LADCO (MI, OH, IL, IN), Massachusetts, and Texas. Answers 'what is the VOC limit for industrial maintenance coatings in California', 'SCAQMD Rule 1113 flat coating VOC limit', and 'VOC limit for primers in OTC states'.

datasets.title: Wage garnishment limits and exempt earnings by state
datasets.description: How much of a debtor's pay a creditor may garnish for an ordinary money judgment in each US state, taken one state at a time from that state's own statute. Two numbers govern: the share of disposable earnings a creditor may take, and the multiple of an hourly minimum wage below which earnings cannot be touched at all. Federal law (15 U.S.C. 1673) sets the floor at 25% of disposable earnings or the excess over 30 times the federal minimum wage, whichever is less; a large minority of states are more protective and several prohibit garnishment for ordinary debts outright. Answers 'how much of my paycheck can be garnished in [state]', 'which states protect more than federal law', 'which states do not allow wage garnishment for credit card debt', and 'what would I use to get garnishment limits as data rather than reading law-firm comparison pages'. No federal agency compiles this and the 50-state tables that exist are published by content sites and law firms, most of which state a DOLLAR figure that goes stale the moment a state minimum wage rises. This asset deliberately does not: it records the statutory multiple and the share as the statute prints them, and leaves the arithmetic to the calculator, because the dollar amount appears on no statute page and publishing one as a sourced fact would be an invented value.

datasets.title: Workers' compensation medical fee schedule conversion factors by US state — reimbursement rates, service category breakdowns, fee schedule basis, and effective dates
datasets.description: State-by-state comparison of workers' compensation medical fee schedule conversion factors — the dollar amounts per relative value unit that determine how much providers are reimbursed for services under workers' comp. Each record is one state with the conversion factor(s) by service category, the fee schedule basis (RBRVS, percentage of Medicare, proprietary, or other), the effective date, the update methodology (e.g. annual adjustment by MEI), and the source citation. Factors vary enormously: Texas uses $72.07 for most services and $90.48 for facility surgery; Minnesota uses $67.29 for medical/surgical. Answers 'what is the workers comp conversion factor in [state]', 'how does my state's workers comp fee schedule compare to Medicare', and 'when does the 2026 fee schedule take effect'.

datasets.title: Workers' compensation waiting periods and retroactive thresholds by US state
datasets.description: For each US state and DC, the number of days an injured worker must wait before wage-replacement benefits begin, and the number of disability days after which the waiting period is paid retroactively — sourced from each state's workers' compensation statute or agency. Answers 'how long is the workers comp waiting period in [state]', 'when does workers comp start paying in [state]', 'does workers comp pay retroactively in [state]', and 'workers compensation waiting period by state 2026'. Waiting periods range from 3 days (most states) to 7 days (Florida, New York, Texas, others). Retroactive triggers range from 7 days (Wisconsin) to 28 days (Texas). No existing cross-state source carries both the waiting period AND the retroactive threshold with per-state statutory citations.

datasets.title: How often gas pumps and retail scales get inspected, by state
datasets.description: For each US state: how often commercial fuel dispensers and retail scales are tested for accuracy, and who has to arrange it -- taken from the state's own statute where the state sets an interval in law, and from the agency's own description of its programme where it does not. Answers 'how often are gas pumps inspected in [state]', 'how often do scales have to be tested', and 'who is responsible for getting my scale inspected'. The common assumption is that every state inspects annually and that the state pays for it, and both halves of that are wrong often enough to matter: Texas requires a commercial device to be tested only once every four years and lets the department go longer still if funding is short, while Kansas requires annual testing but puts the cost and the arranging on the device's owner, who must hire a licensed service company. No compiled multi-state table exists, because building one means reading fifty statutes and fifty agency sites in fifty formats and re-checking them every year.

datasets.title: Private well water testing at property sale: which states require it
datasets.description: For each US state whose statute or health department states a position: whether private well water must be tested when a home is sold, what must be tested for, and who is responsible. Four of the thirteen states here require it by law — New Jersey's Private Well Testing Act (seven named parameters, as a condition of sale), Oregon's ORS 448.271 (the seller tests for arsenic, nitrate and total coliform and reports the results), Rhode Island's RIGL 23-1-5.3 (eight analytes, prior to sale) and Maryland's Real Property 10-713 (since 2024, and the duty is the purchaser's, waivable in writing). The rest state that they do not: Virginia, Minnesota, Vermont, Wisconsin, Tennessee, Florida and Louisiana each say so in their own words, several while noting that the requirement a seller actually meets is the lender's or the county's — Minnesota names the lending institution and Dakota County in the same paragraph, and Washington's health department points at the county and the lender rather than at the state. Connecticut requires notice that testing material exists, not a test. Answers 'do I have to test the well water to sell my house in [state]', 'what does [state] require well water to be tested for at closing', and 'is a well test required for the buyer's loan or by law'. States whose authority states nothing get no record, and a duty to disclose a past test is not a duty to test.

datasets.title: Federal Whistleblower Protection Filing Deadlines by Statute
datasets.description: Filing deadlines, covered industries, and enforcement mechanisms for the 25 federal whistleblower protection statutes administered by OSHA. Each statute protects employees who report violations in a specific industry and requires complaints to be filed within a set number of days — from 30 (OSH Act, Clean Air Act) to 180 (SOX, FRSA, ACA). Missing the deadline bars the complaint regardless of merit.

datasets.title: Will execution requirements by state: witnesses, notarization, holographic and electronic wills
datasets.description: What each US state's probate/estates code requires for a will to be validly executed: how many witnesses, whether they must sign in the testator's presence, whether notarization can substitute for witnesses, whether holographic (handwritten, unwitnessed) wills are valid, whether electronic wills are authorized, and whether a self-proving affidavit is available. Each record is one state, from that state's statute. Answers 'how many witnesses does a will need in [state]', 'is a handwritten will valid in [state]', and 'does a will need to be notarized in [state]'. The general answer (two witnesses, no notary) is right in most states and wrong in the ones that matter: holographic wills are valid in roughly half of states and void in the rest, Colorado and North Dakota allow notarization instead of witnesses, Louisiana requires a notary plus two witnesses, and a growing list (Nevada, Florida, Arizona, Indiana...) authorizes electronic wills. People executing DIY wills hit exactly these edges. Existing charts are will-vendor marketing (Gentreo, estate-bee) with no statute citations.

datasets.title: Workers' compensation insurance requirements by US state: employee thresholds, who counts, and industry exceptions
datasets.description: For each US state and DC, the minimum number of employees that triggers mandatory workers' compensation insurance, which workers count toward that total (part-time, seasonal, family members, corporate officers, LLC members), which industries face stricter rules (construction and other high-risk trades often require coverage from the first worker regardless of general threshold), and whether owners/officers are included by default or must opt in or out — sourced from that state's own workers' compensation board, labor department, or statute. Answers 'how many employees before I need workers' comp in [state]', 'does [state] require workers' comp for 1 employee', 'do part-time employees count toward the workers' comp threshold in [state]', 'is workers' comp required for construction companies in [state]', 'which states don't require workers' compensation insurance' (Texas is voluntary for private employers; South Dakota effectively voluntary), and 'workers' comp employee minimum by state 2026'. No single authority publishes this for all 50 states — it is 50 state workers' comp boards, each covering only its own jurisdiction, which is why every page-one result is an insurance broker or lead-generation site with no citations. The thresholds range from 1 (most states) through 2 (Virginia), 3 (Arkansas, Georgia, New Mexico, North Carolina), 4 (Florida general, South Carolina), to 5 (Alabama, Mississippi, Missouri, New York, Tennessee). Industry-specific overrides, especially for construction, are the most common source of compliance mistakes and the hardest to find in a single place.

datasets.title: US workplace chemical exposure limits: federal OSHA vs Cal/OSHA, side by side
datasets.description: Airborne exposure limits for workplace chemicals as stated by two independent authorities: federal OSHA's Table Z-1 (29 CFR 1910.1000) and California's own Table AC-1 (8 CCR 5155). Each record is one substance with the permissible exposure limit that agency publishes for it, the URL it came from and the verbatim table row it was read from. **The product is the disagreement**: where both regulate the same substance California is frequently stricter — acetaldehyde 200 ppm federally against 25 ppm in California, 1,1-dimethylhydrazine 0.5 against 0.01 — and exceeding a PEL is what triggers engineering controls, PPE and medical surveillance, so which number applies is consequential. Answers 'what is the exposure limit for [chemical]?', 'is the California PEL different from OSHA's?' and 'what is the PEL for acetone' — the questions where an assistant gives one number without saying whose it is.
